title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Elevator State Machine

At every moment, your elevator is in exactly one of five states: IDLE, MOVING, DOORS_OPENING, DOORS_OPEN or DOORS_CLOSING.
Every time round loop(), the code asks: what state am I in, and has anything happened that means I should act or change state? That’s the switch statement in the starter sketch.
A transition is a move from one state to another. It’s triggered by an event (a button press) or a condition (a timer running out, the car reaching a floor).

Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 0: Get connected (5 min?)

Open ElevatorStarter.ino in the Arduino IDE and check that ElevatorHAL.h appears as a second tab.
Upload it, then open Tools → Serial Monitor and set it to 115200 baud.
You should see the car on the ground floor and dim landing lights on all three floors.

Done when: pressing each button prints the right floor number.

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 1: Make it move
When a button is pressed and the elevator is IDLE, the car should travel to that floor and stop. Forget the doors for now.
In the input section, if the state is IDLE, set targetFloor, set direction to +1 (up) or -1 (down), and call changeState(MOVING).
In case MOVING:, use the timer pattern to add direction to carPos every MOVE_STEP_MS. When carPos equals hal_floorPosition(targetFloor), change back to IDLE.
Think: what happens if you press the button for the floor you’re already on? What should happen?
Done when: the car glides to whichever floor you ask for, and presses while it’s moving are ignored.

suggested 20 min

title: Workshop: Going up
section: Task 2: Design the doors on paper
text:
Task 2: Design the doors on paper
Before writing any more code, draw a state diagram. Draw all five states as circles. Draw an arrow for every possible transition and label each arrow with the event or condition that causes it.
Your diagram should answer these questions. What must be true before the car is allowed to move? What happens when the doors finish opening, and when they finish closing? Which states need a timer?
Done when: a demonstrator has checked your diagram.

suggested 10 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 3: Build the doors
Change MOVING so that arriving at the target floor opens the doors instead of going straight to IDLE. Then fill in the three door states, following your diagram:

DOORS_OPENING: every DOOR_STEP_MS, add one to doorOpen. When it reaches DOOR_STEPS, go to DOORS_OPEN.
DOORS_OPEN: once DOOR_HOLD_MS has passed, go to DOORS_CLOSING.
DOORS_CLOSING: every DOOR_STEP_MS, subtract one from doorOpen. When it reaches 0, go to IDLE.

Done when: the car arrives, the doors slide open, wait two seconds, then slide shut, and the Serial Monitor shows the whole sequence of states.

suggested 20 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 4: Remember every call
At the moment, anyone who presses a button while the car is busy is ignored. Real elevators remember.
Replace your Task 1 button code with a single line: calls[f] = true; (you’ll see that floor’s landing lights turn blue). Then move the decision-making into case IDLE:. Look for a floor with a call: if it’s the floor the car is already on, clear the call and open the doors; otherwise set targetFloor and direction and start moving. When the car arrives, clear that floor’s call.
Done when: you can press all three buttons quickly and every floor gets visited, with no blue lights left behind.

suggested 15 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 5: Stop on the way
If the car is travelling from floor 0 to floor 2 and someone on floor 1 presses their button in time, the car should stop at floor 1 first.
In MOVING, after each step, use hal_floorAt(carPos) to find out whether the car is level with a floor. If that floor has a call, stop there.
Done when: test scenarios 3 and 4 behave as expected.

suggested 10 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 6: Choose wisely
When several floors are waiting, which should the car visit next? Write a function int chooseNextCall(int here) that returns a floor number, or -1 if nobody is waiting, and use it in IDLE.
Try at least two of these strategies:

Lowest floor first. Simple, but is it fair?
Nearest floor first.
Keep going the same way while anyone is waiting further along in that direction, and only then turn around. This is known as the elevator algorithm (or SCAN).

Discuss with your partner: can you invent a sequence of button presses where somebody waits forever under one of these strategies? Which would you want in a 50-storey building?

suggested 15 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 7: Make it safe
Hold the doors. If someone presses the button for the floor the car is stopped at while the doors are closing, open them again. If the doors are already fully open, restart the hold timer so they stay open longer.
Check your invariants. An invariant is something that must always be true, no matter what. After the switch, add checks that print a warning to the Serial Monitor if either of these ever happens: the state is MOVING but doorOpen isn’t 0, or carPos is outside the shaft.
Done when: every scenario in the test table below passes with no warnings.

suggested 15 min

delay(2000) freezes the whole Arduino for two seconds. No buttons are read and no LEDs are updated. An elevator that ignored everyone while its doors were open would be a pretty bad elevator.

}

Learning Outcomes

Define a process in the context of operating systems, stating the information the operating system needs to manage a process.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: operating systems


Early computers such as EDSAC had no operating system.











Programmers had to write their programs for the hardware,
Lots of low-level, repeated code,
programs manually loaded by an operator.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: operating systems

Later, a program called the Monitor was introduced.
Allowed scheduling of multiple programs.
All programs had equal access:
possible for one program to overwrite another, even the monitor.
Co-operative multitasking:
a program had to surrender control back to the monitor.
Meant erroneous or malicious programs could crash the whole system.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: operating systems

Hardware support was later added to protect resources:

Instruction levels:
only the Monitor could run privileged instructions.
Memory management unit:
kept track of which areas of memory each process could read, write or execute.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: operating systems

Device drivers to interface with hardware were written,
along with code libraries for common operations.
Linkers and loaders build to allow programs to access external code,
enabling code re-use.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: operating systems

A program responsible for

Managing and protecting resources
e.g., CPU, memory, disk, network.

prevents accidental or malicious damage,
provides efficient use of limited resources.

Providing a programming interface:

written by experts to get best performance out of hardware,
less chance of errors as experts understand the pitfalls,
prevents repeating low-level code.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: operating systems
Desirable attributes:

Lightweight and efficient
so that as many resources as possible can be dedicated to user-land applications.
Flexible and easy to use,
i.e., it should be a help, not a hindrance, to the programmer.

A good operating system is the one you do not notice is there.

title: Processes
text:
Process
Collection of data held by the operating system:

Code (machine instructions),
Data,
Metadata required by the operating system.
Also known as
task, job.
Not to be confused with
processor, program.

title: Processes
text:
Process vs program

A program may consist of several processes.
E.g., one process builds an image, a different process renders it.
Another design pattern enabling separation of concerns,
called structure by process.
Less common in modern computers, which use threads,
although one process is still used for each browser tab, to provide security.

title: Processes
text:
Process metadata
OS requires some information in order to run a process:

where in memory to find the code and data,
memory permissions (i.e., the MMU flags),
allocation (how much CPU time, memory, I/O it is allocated),
usage statistics (how many CPU cycles, how much time),
saved CPU state (e.g., contents of registers).

This allows the OS to manage and protect resources.

title: Processes
text:
Process states

OS keeps track of the state of each process – basic states are

New: a process which has just been created,
OS needs to do some setup,
Running: currently being executed on the CPU,
Ready: waiting to be scheduled, can be run immediately,
blocked: cannot be run because it is waiting for something,
e.g., data to be read from disk,
Exit: process has finished,
OS needs to clean up.

title: Processes
text:
Scheduling


Deciding which process should run next.

I.e., OS moves processes from one state to another.

title: Processes
text:
Process lifecycle

Typically, one process requests creation of another,
called forking or spawning.

E.g., user clicks the web browser icon on their desktop.
Desktop GUI program makes a syscall to the OS,
requesting creation of a new process, running the web browser program.
If allowed, OS creates the new process.
Syscall returns an exit code indicating success or reason for failure.

E.g., no permission to create processes,
Insufficient resources – too many processes running already.

title: Processes
text:
Process lifecycle

All processes start in the new state.
metadata needed to run the process is called the process control block (PCB).

OS initialises process PCB datastructures,
allocates memory,
allocates a process ID (unique identifier for each process),
sets initial priority importance, used by the scheduler),
adds the process to the scheduler’s list,
then moves process to the ready state.

From the ready state,
process can be moved to running when the OS decides to schedule it.

title: Processes
text: Process lifecycle

title: Processes
text:
Process lifecycle

When the OS decides to schedule a process, it is dispatched.
Jump and drop CPU instruction is performed,

Jump to the memory location containing process instructions,
Drop from privileged (only allowed by the OS) mode to unprivileged mode.

A process may voluntarily surrender control,
i.e., relinquish,

save state (of CPU registers, MMU etc),
process moved to ready.

Same happens if the process is interrupted, or its timeslice is over.

title: Processes
text:
Process lifecycle

If the process requires I/O, e.g., read from / write to disk,
it makes a syscall, asking the OS to perform the operation.

state saved, process moved to blocked,

When the operation is complete,

process moved to ready,
will not be running until the OS schedules it.

title: Processes
text:
Process lifecycle

Every process finishes in the exit state.
OS does some cleanup

deallocating memory,
releasing resources (e.g., closing files),
deallocating the process control block.
remove the process from the scheduler’s list.

title: Processes
text:
Process hierarchy

A basic list is not an efficient datastructure for the scheduler.
other representations are preferred, e.g.,

priority queue
process tree.

title: Processes
text:
Process hierarchy

Unix uses a process tree,

first process created, called init is the root of the tree.
new processes become the children of the process which requested their creation,
allows processes to be grouped,
Each group of processes has a process leader.
Processes can be treated as a group,
E.g., killing the process leader causes all processes in its group to be killed, too.

Booting a computer

Process of starting the OS.
Complicated process: needs to identify and set up hardware, load and initialise the OS, start the initial process.
Only then can user-land programs be started.

title: Processes
text:
Booting a computer

Each computer has a small amount of non volatile memory,
flash memory whose data remains saved when there is no power.
On startup, CPU is configured to jump to this memory and begin running instructions.
Tiny program called the bootstrap loader, to load a larger program from other memory
Several rounds of bootstrapping may be needed until we have a program large enough to read from disk.

title: Processes

Bootloader

Program loaded after initial bootstrapping,
Contains instructions to start the OS

may ask the user to choose which OS to start,
knows how to start the OS, and
where to find it, e.g., hard disk or network.

etc/init.d/

title: Architecture overview
text:
Learning Outcomes

State the five components of a Von Neumann computer.
Describe the difference between the Von Neumann and Harvard architecture.
Explain the advantages and disadvantages of the Von Neumann vs Harvard architectures.
Argue for the “best” architecture in a given situation.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Architecture












“Computer architecture, like other architecture, is the art of determining the needs of the user of a structure and then designing to meet those needs as effectively as possible within economic and technological constraints.”
– Frederick P. Brooks


Brooks was an American computer architect, software engineer and computer scientist who managed IBM 360 series of mainframes and their accompanying software.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Computer Architecture

A description of a computer (or computer system) which is made from component parts.
Often a high-level description, indicating how components are linked and what each does.
Sometimes includes details such as the instruction set used and other implementation details.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Computer Architecture

1837: First documented computer architecture was in correspondence between Charles Babbage and Ada Lovelace, where Babbage described his analytical engine.
1890: Herman electromechanical tabulating machine used to analyse census data stored on punched cards.
1936, Conrad Zeus described a computer where both instructions and data are stored in the same memory: First documented instance of a “stored program” or general purpose computer.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Computer Architecture

1945, John Von Neumann described the famous Von Neumann Architecture in his paper on the EDVAC computer (successor to the ENIAC).

title: Architecture overview
text:
Computer Architecture

1946, Alan Turing wrote a detailed proposal for the electronic calculator, Automatic Computing Engine, citing Von Neumann.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Von Neumann Architecture


Arrows represent data transfer connections and directions. I.e., there is an arrow in both directions between the memory and the arithmetic logic unit, representing a “shared bus”. We will see later that this shared bus can be a bottleneck.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Five components

Store
Control Unit
Arithmetic Logic Unit
input
Output

title: Architecture overview
text:
Store

To store data and instructions. E.g., paper tape, magnetic tape, RAM.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Control Unit

decides which instruction to perform next.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Arithmetic Logic Unit

Performs calculations.

Typically the ALU and control unit are combined into the CPU.
Operations performed on the hardware, or implemented in software.
In early computers, electromechanical hardware was used; these days transistors are used, which require much less energy.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Input and Output

Means for the user to interact with the computer.

Keyboard, mouse, camera, sensors.
Monitor, speakers.
Varied and interesting ways for humans and computers to interact.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Key features

Instructions and data are stored in the same memory.
Simple, cost-effective and widely used.



Single bus to transfer all data.
This can cause a bottleneck.
Sequential architecture Can limit speed of processing. : CPU can perform only one instruction at a time.
This is the architecture found in most desktop PCs today.

title: Architecture overview
text: Harvard Architecture

title: Architecture overview
text:
Harvard Architecture

Has separate memory for instructions and data.
Well suited to embedded systems and main-frames.



Reduces the memory bottleneck found in Von Neumann machines.

Less contention as there is no shared bus.
Data and instruction access can be done simultaneously.
Less flexible than Von-Neumann. E.g., instructions cannot be modified at run-time.

title: Architecture overview
text:
In small groups

In which situations is each architecture used?

Today and historically?
Why is it a good choice for that situation, or why not?

Things to think about:

where are the bottlenecks?
special purpose vs general purpose
data integrity / tampering / security

title: Architecture overview
text:
1949

“The”brain” [computer] may one day come down to our level [of the common people] and help with our income-tax and book-keeping calculations. But this is speculation and there is no sign of it so far.”

– British newspaper The Star in a June 1949 news article about the EDSAC computer.

title: Architecture overview
text:
1953

“I think there is a world market for maybe five computers.”

– Thomas Watson, IBM Chairman, although this is now thought to be urban legend.

The “brain” computer has now very much “come down to the level of the common people”, and does much more than just book-keeping.
Regarding the Watson quote, it is now thought to be an urban legend. see https://geekhistory.com/content/urban-legend-i-think-there-world-market-maybe-five-computers
“We believe the statement that you attribute to Thomas Watson is a misunderstanding of remarks made at IBM’s annual stockholders meeting on April 28, 1953. In referring specifically and only to the IBM 701 Electronic Data Processing Machine – which had been introduced the year before as the company’s first production computer designed for scientific calculations – Thomas Watson, Jr., told stockholders that “IBM had developed a paper plan for such a machine and took this paper plan across the country to some 20 concerns that we thought could use such a machine. I would like to tell you that the machine rents for between $12,000 and $18,000 a month, so it was not the type of thing that could be sold from place to place. But, as a result of our trip, on which we expected to get orders for five machines, we came home with orders for 18.” https://geekhistory.com/content/urban-legend-i-think-there-world-market-maybe-five-computers

title: Architecture overview
text:
Learning Outcomes

Give an overview of early computers: use, specs, how they were programmed.
Compare early and modern computers
Explain how developments in early computing have influenced modern computer hardware.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Integers

We already saw that an unsigned integer number can be represented in Binary.
Usually the right-most bit represents the least significant digit.
Little-endian representation.
Signed integers may be represented in several ways:

Sign+magnitude: one bit is reserved for the sign, the rest for the value.
This representation allows \(+0\) and \(-0\).
One’s complement: positive numbers represented as usual, negative numbers represented by flipping all their bits.
Again, we have \(+0\) and \(-0\).
Two’s complement: positive numbers represented as usual, negative numbers represented by adding one then flipping all their bits.
only one \(0\), no redundancy.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Floating point numbers

IEEE 754 defines a standard for representing and manipulating floating point numbers.
Represented in a similar way to scientific notation.
E.g., \(300,000,000 = 3 \times 10^8\).

The \(3\) is called the fraction (coefficient or mantissa).
The \(8\) (from \(10^8\)) is called the exponent.

IEEE 754 defines:

The base, typically \(2\) for binary, but sometimes \(10\).
Precision (number of digits to represent the fraction).
An exponent range.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Floating point numbers

Using \(n\) bits, the representation consists of

\(1\) bit for the sign,
\(n - p - 1\) bits for the exponent.
\(p\) bits for the fraction (stored in Binary),

Any signed number up to \(p\) significant digits and a maximum exponent of \(n-p-1\) can be defined.
Positive and negative infinity.
A representation for not a number, e.g., for the result of division by zero.

title: Architecture overview
text:
32-bit floating point
Representation used for the float type in many programming languages.


\(32\) bits:

\(1\) bit for the sign,
\(8\) bits for the exponent,
\(23\) bits for the fraction.

Around \(7\) decimal digits for the fraction.
A double uses \(64\) bits, \(52\) bits (around \(16\) decimal digits).

title: Architecture overview
text:
Floating point numbers
Advantages

Efficient representation of very large and very small numbers.
Fast computation due to many years of hardware development.

Disadvantages

Floating point errors.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Precision and accuracy

Precision: how many significant digits,
Accuracy: how close to the true value.

A value may be precise but not accurate, accurate but not precise, or both inaccurate and imprecise.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Floating point errors

We know that \(1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1\).
However, \(0.3333333333 + 0.3333333333 + 0.3333333333 = 0.9999999999\)!
\(1/10\) is easy to represent in decimal: \(0.1\).
However, in binary, it is \(0.001100110011\).
Floating point representation is sufficient for most applications, e.g., 3D games.
However, we have to take care with things like currency, which must be correct.

title: Architecture overview
section: But first, why are we doing this?
text:
But first, why are we doing this?

Gain perspective.
Understanding of why things are the way they are today.
Learn from previous successes and failures.

title: Architecture overview
text:
The ENIAC (1945)


Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer

Special purpose computer for artillery firing table calculations.
Located at the School of Engineering and Applied Science, Pennsylvania State University














Could be “programmed” by using the plug-board and switches, data entered via punched cards.
Later converted into a stored program computer.
Base-10 arithmetic instead of the usual binary.
Used vacuum tubes, which burnt out often – high maintenance.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Colossus (1943-45)













Special purpose computer developed at Bletchley Park to help break the Lorenz cipher.
Designed by Tommy Flowers, a research engineer at the General Post Office, based on plans by Code and Cipher School mathematician Max Newman.




Used vacuum tubes; programmed using switches and a plug board.
Data memory was a cycling strip of paper tape.
Colossus Mk II, which used shift registers to run 6 times faster, went into operation in time for the D-day landings.
By the end of the war, 10 Colossi were in operation.

title: Architecture overview
text:
General purpose computers (post WW2)
Von Neumann arranged a 6-week summer workshop to design and build a new type of computer.

General purpose: many early computers were designed with a specific task in mind, which meant they were difficult to repurpose.
Von Neumann wanted to build a stored program computer.
Electronic:replacing electromechanical components which were brittle, hot and noisy.
Colossus and the ENIAC both consumed 150KW of power.
Use binary, which is the easiest encoding to work with when using electronic components.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Maurice Wilkes

Cambridge mathematician, physics PhD on “radio propagation of very long radio waves in the ionosphere”.
Attended Jon Neumann’s workshop, then returned to Cambridge to build the EDSAC machine.
Worked in radar during WW2, which inspired the memory technology for EDSAC.
Memory was a limitation for early electronic computers, Wilkes used “delay lines”, mercury tubes and an oscilloscope, as memory.


More information on mercury delay lines: Radar pulses were captured and played as sound waves. Sound waves passed through mercury, which slowed them down. Picked up by a microphone and displayed no an oscilloscope screen. Sound wave amplified and played back through the speaker so the pulse would repeat as long as needed.

title: Architecture overview
text:
EDSAC (6 May 1949)


Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator

One of the first stored program computers which used binary.
Developed by Maurice Wilkes, William Renwick (hardware engineer) and David Wheeler (first system software engineer).














Could perform 700 additions or 200 multiplications per second.
512 18-bit words of memory for programs and data, upgraded to 1024 18-bit words in 1952.
Data and programs were loaded via 5-hole punched paper tape, initial orders instructed the computer to load the program.
Consumed 11KW of power.
The delay line memory was sub-optimal, but one of the best options at the time.
Although the words were 18-bits, only 17 bits were used in practice owing to unreliability of memory. ## Programming the EDSAC
Programs designed on paper and then punched, in assembler, onto 5-hole paper tape. Programmers became proficient at reading programs from the tape.
Programmers would hang their tape on a line, waiting for an operator to run them – the first “job queue”.
Operator would load program and data and then either return the printed output or inform the programmer of the memory address at which the program failed. ## Operating EDSAC
Built-in add, multiply, bus and conditional jump.

No load. Instead, Instead clear the register (set to \(0\)) and add the value from memory to the register.
No division, but it was included as a subroutine.

In case of a program error, the operator would inform the programmer at which address their program failed.
There was no debugger. An oscilloscope screen showed the state of the registers, and a speaker played a different note depending on the value of the accumulator register. An experienced programmer learnt the sound of a failing program, e.g., if there was an infinite loop. ## Operating EDSAC
Programmers had to use “bad” programming technique. E.g., to access a different array element, the code would modify itself to point to the correct address.
No built-in mechanism for subroutines, instead perform a Wheeler jump: Jump with return memory address, computer would modify the last instruction of the subroutine to jump back to this return address.- No recursion was possible on the EDSAC. Turing proposed the call stack in his 1945 paper, which implemented subroutines “properly” and allowed recursion.

A condition for funding was that EDSAC must provide a service, as opposed to just being an engineering experiment.

Ronald Fisher, with Wilkes and Wheeler, used EDSAC to solve a differential equation for gene frequency – first use of computers in biology.
In 1951, Miller and Wheeler computed a 79-digit prime number, the largest known at its time.
EDSAC played a role in Nobel-prize-winning research: Nobel laureates thanked EDSAC in their acceptance speech. John Kendrew and Max Perutz (Chemistry, 1962), Andrew Huxley (Medicine, 1963) and Martin Ryle (Physics, 1974)
EDSAC remained in operation until 11 July 1958, when it was superseded by EDSAC 2, which ran until 1965.

title: The CPU
text:
Recap: Harvard architecture


Recall the control unit, arithmetic logic unit, input and output. Harvard architecture has separate memory for programs and data, and a separate bus. This meant there was less contention as instructions and data could be accessed simultaneously, but the machine was less flexible, e.g., the program memory may not be full when data memory is, but we cannot use the free space in the program memory for additional data. This architecture commonly used in embedded systems, and mainframes.

title: The CPU
text:
The Von Neumann Architecture


Same components: control unit, arithmetic logic unit, input and output. In the Harvard architecture, data and instructions are stored in the same memory. A single memory bus can be a bottleneck, and concerns were raised about security (e.g., a program can write to any location in memory, including modifying the instructions. Simpler and more flexible. This is the architecture found in most desktop computers today.

A program, written in assembler, is a sequence of instructions.

The CPU has a small number of registers (R1, R2, and R3 on the picture) to store intermediate values.
There is also a small amount of very fast memory, the cache, located either on or very near the CPU.

title: The CPU
section: The Fetch, decode, execute store Cycle
text:
The Fetch, decode, execute store Cycle
A CPU goes through four stages to run an instruction:

title: The CPU
text:
Fetch



First stage of the cycle.
Program counter points to the memory address of the next instruction.
Retrieve the next instruction from memory and store it in the instruction register.
Increment the program counter to point to the next instruction.

title: The CPU
text:
Decode



The control unit reads the current instruction in the instruction register.
The control unit determines which operation(s) to perform.
If the instruction has operands the control unit initiates additional fetches to retrieve these from memory.











The CPU is now ready to execute the instruction.

title: The CPU
text:
Execute



The stage at which operations are performed.
The ALU performs the decoded operation with its operands.
In more advanced CPUs may have special-purpose hardware, e.g., a floating point unit.
Instruction may load data from memory into a register.
May perform a jump (e.g., conditional or loop) – program counter is set to point to a different instruction.











Any return value is stored in a register. Ready for the next stage…

title: The CPU
text:
Interrupt

Occasionally, the CPU receives an interrupt signal.
The CPU immediately stops executing the current instruction and jumps to an interrupt service routine.
The interrupt service routine is just another set of instructions stored in memory.
The CPU executes these instructions as usual, then jumps back to the instruction it was previously working on.
If the instruction was interrupted halfway through, then the CPU must restart it from the beginning.

title: The CPU
text:
The Little man Computer



Simple model of a Von Neumann architecture computer.
Imagine a “Little Man” trapped inside a locked mail room.
The mail room has 100 mailboxes labelled 00-99, each of which can hold a 3 decimal digit instruction or data.












Input is received via an inbox and output returned via an outbox.
There is a work area with a simple addition and subtraction, the accumulator.
There is a program counter which tells the Little Man from which address to fetch the next instruction.

title: The CPU
text:
How it works

The Little Man checks the program counter and retrieves the instruction at the specified address.
The program counter is incremented so that it points to the address (mailbox) containing the next instruction.
Little Man decodes the instruction.


Op-code: number from 000-999 which tells the Little Man what operation to perform.
If data is required, its mailbox address is included in the instruction.


If required, data is fetched from the mailbox referred in the instruction.
Execute the instruction.
Branch (change the value in the program counter) or store the result of the instruction.
Repeat or halt.

title: The CPU
text:
Instruction set architectures

Each processor architecture has its own instruction set:
A set of op-codes which the control unit interprets as instructions.
There are two main types of instruction set architecture

RISC: reduced instruction set computer, and
CISC: complex instruction set computer.

title: The CPU
text:
History

Up to the early 80’s, more instructions were being added to processors.
Designers wanted to mimic high-level programming languages.
One CPU instruction should be one line of source code.
Offload more work onto the hardware.
Produce shorter programs (fewer total instructions) to conserve memory.

title: The CPU
text:
History

In the early 80’s, the idea of creating a smaller and simple set of instructions was proposed.
Aim was to make designing and building a CPU easier, cheaper and, therefore, faster.
Term RISC coined by David Patterson, a researcher at UC Berkeley.

title: The CPU
text:
RISC: reduced instruction set computer
Small, simple set of instructions, e.g., as found in the Little Man computer.

Processor can execute exactly one instruction per cycle.
Instructions are a fixed length (fixed number of bits).
Can only manipulate values stored in CPU registers.
RISC chips are simple to design and cheap to build.
Used in ARM-based chips, found in microcontrollers (Arduino, Raspberry Pi) and smartphones.
Also used in IBM Power processors (used in mainframes and servers).

title: The CPU
text:
CISC: complex instruction set computing
Large number of instructions, some performing more complicated operations – intended to correspond to statements in a high-level programming language.

Variable-length instructions.
May take multiple clock cycles to execute an instruction.
Able to manipulate values directly in main memory.
CISC chips are complex, with special-purpose hardware, and are more expensive to build.
Found in most PCs – the x86 architecture.

text:
Second-generation of computers

Recall that early computers, e.g., EDSAC, used vacuum tubes (thermionic valves).
These were bulky, unreliable, generated lots of heat and required lots of energy to run.
In the late 1950s, computers began to use electronic circuit boards made out of transistors instead.
These computers were popular until the late 1960s.

Developed at the University of Manchester
Working prototype in November 1953,
had 92 transistors and 950 diodes.
Full-size version was operational in 1955
had 200 transistors, 1300 diodes and consumed 150W of power.
Early transistors were unreliable. Average error-free runtime was 1.5 hours.

Third generation computers

Widely used from the mid 60s to early 70s.
Used integrated circuits (ICs)
An IC is a single chip containing all transistors, resistors, capacitors, diodes and connections needed to operate.
Invented by Jack Kilby in 1958, an electrical engineer working at Texas Instruments.
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000.
Faster and more reliable than second generation.
Reduced computing time from micro seconds to nano seconds.
Computers were becoming more compact, affordable and easy to use with high-level programming languages and mouse and keyboard instead of punched cards.

Moore’s “Law”

Prediction made by Gordon Moore, co-founder of Intel, in 1965:
“Number of transistors per chip doubles every two years.”


Note that it’s not a “law” as in “law of physics”. More of a prediction which has remained (mostly) true.

text:
Dennard scaling

Stated in a 1974 paper co-authored by Robert H. Dennard:
“As transistors get smaller, their power density stays constant – power use stays in proportion with area.”
If a transistor is 30% smaller, then its power consumption is 30% less.
An IC of fixed size with twice the number of transistors consumes the same power.
Allowed manufacturers to significantly increase clock speed without increase power consumption.

title: The CPU
text:
Dennard scaling



Appears to have broken down since 2006.
Since 2016 the number of transistors per chip is still growing, but more slowly.
As transistors get smaller, current leakage and heat production is more problematic.












We see clock speed plateau – as clack speed increases it becomes more difficult to cool the chip.
This is called the power wall.

We are no longer able to double the number of transistors per chip.
Transistors are still getting smaller and more tightly packed, but progress is becoming slower.

Recap: scheduling

Deciding which process should run next.
We studied many scheduling algorithms, the most complex of which was
Traditional Unix Scheduling.
A pre-emptive scheduler.
Process priority computed every second from a
base value, CPU used and optional nice value.
System processes have more base priority.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Recap: scheduling

Used in early Unix systems and Windows NT.
However, not suitable for modern operating systems,
since it does not scale well to large numbers of processes.
Priorities are recalculated all at once, every second.

Takes a significant amount of CPU time,
Is not done often enough to reflect changes in behaviour.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Recap: pitfalls of processes
As well as scheduling processes, the OS also has to:

Prevent deadlocks,
all processes waiting for one of their number to do something.
Process protection:
insuring that processes cannot interfere with one another.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Recap: process protection

Recall that each process is owned by a user.
A user can mess with their own processes, but not the processes of other users.
Provides security.
A special user, called root can mess with the processes of all users.
The MMU also provides a hardware solution to prevent one process from accessing another process’s memory.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Inter-process communication

The OS works hard to isolate processes from each another.
What happens if one process needs to communicate with another?
E.g., one process may need to tell another that a particular job, e.g., disk write, is done.
Or a new process may need to tell the Window Manager to make a new GUI window.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Inter-process communication

OS facilitates communication between processes,
but takes care to do this safely.
Many methods of IPC, we will study a few:

Files,
Pipes,
Shared Memory,
Signals,
Semaphores.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Files



Possibly the simplest method of IPC,
since it uses an existing mechanism.

Process \(A\) writes data to a file,
Process \(B\) reads the data.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Files

Which file should be used?

Communal IPC file,
but if more than two processes are sharing data, how do we tell which bytes are meant for which process.
Then use one file per pair of processes,
but some prior communication is needed to agree on a file.

How does process \(B\) know when process \(A\) is finished writing?
File permissions must be set correctly,
so that the OS will allow both processes to access the file.
Useful for sharing large amounts of data.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Pipes

Two-ended, FIFO data structure.
Allows output of one process to be used as input of another.




FIFO: first in, first out. Queue.
You mau would have encountered this in a queue (real world and the datastructure), also pipelines.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Pipes

Allow sharing data, similar to files,
but provide synchronisation, too.

Process \(A\) writes to the pipe,
Pipe becomes full (pipe can usually hold 4096 bytes)
Process \(A\) is blocked, process \(B\) is scheduled,
Process \(B\) reads data from the pipe,
When the pipe is empty, process \(B\) is blocked.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Pipes

FIFO: data is read in the same order as it is written.
Pipes are unidirectional (data flows in one direction), but two-way communication can be achieved with two pipes.
Pipes affect scheduling, as they can block processes:
it’s possible to cause a circular wait with two pipes.
Implemented as a buffer (block of memory managed by the OS).

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Exercise: POSIX pipes

In Unix, the | character creates a pipe between two processes.
E.g., on the command line, $ ls -1 | grep foo

$ is the shell prompt.
ls -1 lists all files in the current directory, one per line,
| takes this list of files (output of ls -1) and passes it to the next process,
grep foo filters the input, returning only lines containing foo – in this case, it filters the files.

play with pipes!
Check out this article on processes and pipes.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Shared Memory



Similar to files, multiple processes read from / write to the same chunk of memory.
Modern OSs prevent usually prevent this, so it has to be set up and managed by the OS.
But shared memory is much faster than files.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Shared Memory

Same drawbacks as with files:

Where is the shared memory,
When should process \(B\) start reading,
I.e., how does it know that process \(A\) has finished writing.
Authorisation: \(A\), \(B\) and no other processes should have access to the shared memory.

Despite the drawbacks, it is still widely used due to its speed,
but it is used alongside other synchronisation mechanisms.



needs synchronisation mechanisms, e.g., semaphores, which we’ll talk about shortly.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Signals

Software equivalent of hardware interrupts, i.e.,

process receives a signal,
stops what it is doing, saves its state, and
jumps to a signal handler.

The signal handler is a piece of code, written by the programmer.



We said “the program stops what it’s doing, saves it’s state and jumps…” but really the OS manages all of this.

OS is responsible for sending, receiving and handling (either doing something or passing on to the process) all signals.
What really happens:
Signal dispatched (raised) via a syscall to the OS.
Signal is flagged in the receiving processes PCB (process control block).
Next time the receiving process is scheduled, the OS observes the signal flag and jumps to the signal handling code.
Once the signal is handled, the flag is removed so that next time the process is scheduled it runs from where it left off, before the signal was handled.
note that this means the programmer has to be careful when writing their code as signals can come at any time, so their program could be interrupted at any moment, and they have to be aware of any changes the signal handler has made.
concurrent programming is difficult and should be a module in its own right!

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Signals

The OS only allows signals to be sent to processes with the same user ID.
Admin (the root user) can send signals to any process.
The OS itself can send signals, too,
e.g., to indicate that a peripheral is ready.



remember that signals are handled by the OS, so when we say “process sends a signal”, we mean it makes a syscall and the OS handles the signal. OS performs user ID checking to see if the signal is permitted.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Signals

All signals must go through the OS.

Provides protection:
e.g., user ID checking.
Some signals have specific behaviour which cannot be overridden,
e.g., KILL signal causes a process to be terminated immediately.
Signals are used by the OS if a process has done something bad, e.g.,

accessed memory it is not allowed to (SIGSEGV, segmentation fault),
tried to run a privileged operation (SIGILL, illegal instruction),





Note that some signals can be handled, or ignored, by the program.
Others, e.g., KILL, SEGV, are handled by the operating system and usually result in the process being terminated.
It is clear that one user shouldn’t be able to signal other users’ processes.
This would allow one user to terminate another user’s processes.
It’s also a reminder not to run as root unless you really need to, since you could accidentally do this!

Widely used,
They are fast and efficient,
Only send a small amount of data,
Asynchronous (can be sent / received at any time),
which means they can be fiddly to program.
Often used in conjunction with other IPC techniques,

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Semaphores



A flag (variable) allowing synchronisation of processes.
Another great invention of Dijkstra, who wrote
“Go to sleep, we’ll wake you up again when you need to continue.”
Two actions:

Wait (P) (also signal, post, raise, up and unlock),
Signal (V) (also lower, down, lock).

Exercise: find out what P and V stand for – Dijkstra is Dutch.












Likely unrelated to the flag language;
probably from the Greek “apparatus for signalling”.*




Dijkstra, very famous Dutch computer scientist. We met him already when discussing the Bankers algorithm, but he’s perhaps most famous for his shortest path algorithm.
Unfortunately, it’s probably not related to the flag language, a better analogy might be a railway signal. I.e., the train waits until they are signalled to go.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Semaphores

One process often needs to tell another that it has finished a task,
semaphores allow this.
E.g., \(A\) writes to an area of shared memory, then signals process \(B\) using a semaphore,
process \(B\) waits for the semaphore, which opens when \(A\) has finished with the memory.



signal with a semaphore means “do the raise, up, or V operation”, and is not related to OS signals.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Semaphores

Provide synchronisation and mutual exclusion.
E.g., a train arrives at a Railway Semaphore,




Attempts to lower (wait) for the Semaphore,
Another train is using the track, so the operation is blacked and the train must wait.
When track becomes free, semaphore is raised (signalled),
Train lowers the semaphore and use the track,
When finished, semaphore is raises.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Semaphores vs signals

OS signals are designed to alert a process of a specific event,
e.g., a key press, or invalid memory access.
Semaphores are specifically designed to implement
synchronisation and mutual exclusion.
A semaphore allows the process to “wait” for a certain event,
e.g., a write to shared memory.
Semaphores are atomic,

I.e., no scheduling happens between checking and setting the value of a semaphore.
Ensures no changes happen between checking and setting.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Exercise: counting semaphore



Counting semaphore:

The semaphore can be raised (or signalled) \(N\) times,
Then it can be lowered (or waited on) \(N\) times.

Solve the dining philosophers problem using a counting semaphore.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Semaphores

Can be implemented in hardware or software.
E.g., there are specific CPU instructions.
Very fast with hardware support.
Can be used to protect shared resources,
both in the OS and in user-land.
They are low-level and easy to get wrong:
it’s easy to cause accidental deadlock.

title: Intr-Process Communication
text:
Synchronisation mechanisms

Some consider semaphores to be too low-level and complicated and proposed alternative approaches:

Condition variables can be used to tell a process when to proceed,
Barriers ensure all processes reach the same point in the code before any of them can continue (a synchronisation point),
Monitors are an object-orientated approach for indicating critical regions of code.




a critical region is a block of code which must be run all at once, with no scheduling, or multi-threading.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Registers

Small blocks of memory located on the CPU itself.
Used to store intermediate values as the CPU works on them.
Very fast, direct access by the CPU with no latency.
Examples: IR, PC, accumulator.
Modern CPUs often have severaal registers.
Fastest and most expensive type of memory
Very limited capacity – in the order of bytes.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Cache

Small, fast memory located claso to the CPU.
Intermediate storage between CPU and main memory:
smaller and faster than main memory, slower and larger than registers.
Multiple levels of cache:
L1 is the fastest, smallest and closest to the CPU.
Still expensive, therefore limited size – in the order of kilo to mega-bytes.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Main memory

Random access memory — each byte can be accessed with the same latency.
Very slow in comparison to cache.
Comparatively large capacity – in the order of giga-bytes.
Data and programs are loaded into memory from disk.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Volatile Memory

Registers, cache and main memory are volatile:
data is lost when power is lost.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Disk

The slowest and largest type of memory.
Much slower than main memory.
Persistent storage: data is preserved if power is lost.
Punched cards, then magnetic tape were used in early computers.
Later, magnetic spinning disks, hard disk drives (HDDs), were used.
Modern computers use flash memory: solid state drives (SSDs).

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Network

Allows access to data on other computers.
Early machines used coaxial cable, later twisted pair Ethernet.
Modern computers use fibre-optic cable or radio waves Wi-Fi.
Orders of magnitude slower than disk.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Analogy: let’s bake a cake


Imagine you’re plannning to bake a cake.










You have a limited number of bowls to weigh and mix ingredients,



A moderate amount of work surface to place items on,
and storage cupboards where large bags of ingredients are kept.













We will build a real-world analogy of computer memory by talking about making a cake.
Mixing bowls, spoons, measuring jug con be used to model CPU registers.
The work surface can be thought of as the cache – items can be easily accessed.
The storage cupboard can be veiwed as main memory, where items can be readily accessed, but more time and effort is needed to locate the item than simply picking it up from the work surface.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Load from memory into registers



Fetch the butter from the fridge
and sugar from the cupboard.
Measure butter and sugar into a mixing bowl.
Cream together butter and sugar.














Fetching ingredients from cupboard / fridge is the same idea as loading data from main memory into the cache (work sorface).
Measuring out ingredients is similar to loading values from cache into CPU registers (the mixing bowl).
The process of creaming together butter and sugar is something like the CPU operating on its data in registers.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Add eggs



Fetch eggs from the fridge…
But you realise there are no eggs left.
Fortunately, you keep chickens and they are laying well.
Go to the end of the garden and collect some eggs.
Returning from the chicken coop, you place the eggs on the work surface.














Rather than fetching from the comparatively quick main memory (cupboard / fridge), you have to do a “read from disk” – walk down the garden, go into the chicken coop and locate the eggs. This is comparatively much slower than retrieving something from the nearby cupboard.

Little aside on pre-fetching. - Had you known in advance there were no eggs in main memory, you could have optimised: - Ask your friend to collect eggs while you are mixing butter and sugar. You will be ready for the eggs, which they loaded into cache (put on the worktop), or better still, cracked straight into the mixing bowl as they return (load directly into registers), for your use.

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Add flour and bake



Fortunately, there is plenty of flour in the store cupboard.
Fetch the sack of flour, weigh it into the mixing bowl and fold it into the mixture.
Scoop the mixture into cake tins and bake in the oven.













7, 8. Similar to the butter and sugar situation, a relatively quick read from memory. 9. The oven is a bit like a co-processor. You can offload a particular task onto it and use the main CPU to do other things (you can prepare the butter cream / frosting while the cake bakes).

title: Memory Architecture
text:
Cream and jam



While the cake is cooling, you decide to whip the cream.
There is no cream or jam in the fridge.
You need to go to the shop.


This takes much longer even than fetching eggs from the garden.
So long that the cake is already cool.












You return from the shop and place the cream and jam on the work surface.




is analogous to fetching data from the network.

going to the shop, on the other hand, is much farther and takes much longer. it also requires a different protocol (choosing items, paying for items) than fetching something locally.

Learning Outcomes

title: Processes
text:
Recap: operating systems

A program responsible for

Managing and protecting resources
e.g., CPU, memory, disk, network.

prevents accidental or malicious damage,
provides efficient use of limited resources.

Providing a programming interface:

written by experts to get best performance out of hardware,
less change of errors as experts understand the pitfalls,
prevents repeating low-level code.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: operating systems
Desirable attributes:

Lightweight and efficient
so that as many resources as possible can be dedicated to user-land applications.
Flexible and easy to use,
i.e., it should be a help, not a hindrance, to the programmer.

A good operating system is tho one you do not notice is there.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: Processes
Collection of data held by the operating system:

Code (machine instructions),
Data,
Metadata required by the operating system.
Not to be confused with a program,
which may consist of several processes.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: processes
OS requires some information in order to run a process:

where in memory to find the code and data,
memory permissions (i.e., the MMU flags),
allocation (how much CPU time, memory, I/O it is allocated),
usage statistics (how many CPU cycles, how much time),
some other information, used for scheduling,
saved CPU state (e.g., contents of registers).

This allows the OS to manage and protect resources.

along with state information, e.g., MMU flags and CPU registers, the OS keeps statistics used by the scheduler. We will discuss these in more detail shortly.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: processes

in Unix, processes are represented as a tree,
an initial process, called init is at the root,
when a new process is created, its parent is usually the process which requested its creation.
tree structure allows processes to be grouped, and managed as groups.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: bootstrapping

Starting the OS and creating the initial process.
Has to identify and initialise hardware,
locate and load the operating system.
requires a small amount of non-volatile memory to store a bootstrapping program.
may take several rounds of bootstrapping before the OS is loaded from disk.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: processes

One process may ask the OS to create a new one (fork or spawn),
OS creates a process in the new state.
When a process is initialised, the OS moves it to the ready state.
The OS may decide to schedule (dispatch) a ready process,
its state is changed to running and any saved data is restored (MMU, registers).
if a process requires I/O, it requests this from the OS via a syscall,
OS sets its state to blocked until the I/O is done, then its state i set to ready.

title: Processes
text:
Recap: processes

A running process may be interrupted or pre-empted,
then its data is saved and state changed to ready.
When a process is finished, its state is set to exit,
the OS does some cleanup before the process is deleted.

title: Processes
text:
Scheduling


Deciding which process should run next.

I.e., OS moves processes from one state to another.

title: Processes
text:
Scheduling

A hard problem!
People are still searching for a solution to satisfy everyone.
Lots of requirements, some of them are conflicting.
Many solutions proposed so far,
we’ll look at some scheduling algorithms shortly.

title: Processes
text:
A scheduler should

not give any process too much CPU, but
not give any process too little, either (starvation).
Give compute-heavy processes longer, larger slices of CPU time, but
give interactive processes small slices of CPU time very often.
Ensure real-time (safety-critical) processes run immediately.
Ensure optimum use of hardware,
everything should be busy, nothing should be waiting.
Optimise for different types of hardware, e.g.,
mice and printers are slow, network and disk is (comparatively) fast.

title: Processes
text:
A scheduler should

Provide predictable behaviour, and
degrade gracefully under excessive load.
Run fast, so as to maximise time spent running user-land applications
and avoid thrashing.

title: Processes
text:
A scheduler should



Note that other resources, e.g., I/O, need scheduling, too.
The different resource schedulers may disagree about which process to run next.

title: Processes
text:
Long, medium and short-term scheduling
We can divide scheduling up into three categories:

long-term: which processes can be admitted
(e.g., is there enough memory),
Medium: what to load into memory, ready to run,
Short: what process to run next.

title: Processes
text:
Long, medium and short-term scheduling



Short-term scheduler is given a list of processes to choose from
by the medium term scheduler.
Medium-term scheduler is given a list of processes by the short-term scheduler.

title: Processes
text:
Long, medium and short-term scheduling

Long-term scheduling was important in the 60s, when resources were scarce.
It is becoming less relevant now, particularly as we have virtual resources.
Medium-term scheduling is still important, involves deciding what to load into memory.
We will study this when we look at memory management.
Short-term scheduling decides which, of a list of ready processes, to execute on the CPU next.
We will now study some simple scheduling algorithms.

title: Processes
text:
Collecting information about processes

We need to give each process a score to help decide which to run next.
Score may be calculated based on:

resources used (CPU, memory),
outcomes, e.g., throughput, turnaround,
real-time, e.g., in control systems,
money, e.g., in time-sharing clusters.

all this information is stored in the PCB.



reminder: throughput is how many jobs done per unit time.
turnaround is a measure of how quickly something responds.
keep track of money in time-sharing systems: some users may pay more for more resources of a faster turnaround time.
reminder: PCB is process control block.

title: Processes
text:
Collecting information about processes



Early computers were shared resources,
users would pay for time.
Less relevant with PCs,
However, still important in cloud computing,
e.g., AWS, Azure bill for processing time, network / storage / memory used.













Replace AWS with Claude / Gemini / ChatGPT.

title: Processes
text:
Exercise: to reflect on
“There is nothing new in computer science, just recurring fashions.”

Think about, and discuss the above.
Other than early time-sharing computers vs cloud computing services, can you think of any other examples of recurring fashions?
Are there any completely new trends?

title: Processes
text:
Scheduling algorithms

There are many, many different algorithms.
Being a complicated task, some of these are complicated algorithms.
Let’s take a look at some of the simplest.

title: Processes
text:
Run Until Completion
Run every program until finished, programs wait in a queue.

best for large, compute-intensive tasks,
no scheduling overheads (OS does not have to decide what to do),
poor utilisation of resources, i.e., no spooling.
Cannot process while printing; cannot print while processing.
No interactivity.
Poorly suited to desktops,
but still widely used in large time-sharing (often distributed) clusters, e.g., to run jobs for scientific research.



queue in computer science is a first-in-first-out datastructure.

title: Processes
text:
Shortest Job First
Shortest (estimated) time to finish goes next.

No pre-emption, same as RTC.
Good throughput, with a similar performance to RTC.
Large jobs (long time remaining) become starved,
May be hard (difficult to get right, and computationally intensive) to estimate time remaining.



RTC: run (un)til completion

title: Processes
text:
Run Until Completion + Co-operative Multitasking
Same as RTC, but processes can voluntarily relinquish control back to the OS.

when a process relinquishes, another process is scheduled.
Maybe in a round-robin fashion, or something more sophisticated, e.g., shortest time remaining.
Poor utilisation of hardware, as parallelism is still not possible.
Poor interactivity.
Voluntary nature causes many problems,
e.g., one program may monopolise all resource (either accidentally or on purpose).



as we discussed in the history section, cooperative programming is difficult.
it’s hard to write a “good citizen” program, which treats others fairly, and it’s also easy to be selfish and monopolise all resources.
interactivity and good use of hardware (parallelism) is difficult as the programmer has no knowledge what others are doing, e.g., “I’d have let you go now if I had known your disk read is done.”

title: Processes
text:
Pre-emptive Round Robin
Each process given a timeslice in round-robin fashion.

Early form of multitasking,
better interactivity.
Each process gets a turn, so no starvation,
Compute intensive and I/O intensive processes both have the same amount of time,
although we know this is not optimal.
Unsuitable for real-time processes, which cannot wait their turn.

Works best when all processes have the same priority, e.g., in network routing devices.

title: Processes
text:
Tweaking round-robin

Pre-emptive scheduling is a good idea,
so maybe we just need to improve upon round robin?
When tweaking, it is important to understand what you are doing.
It is easy to write a large, slow scheduler which is impossible to understand.
Then it’s impossible to fix when you find an inefficiency.

We can improve upon round robin by taking priority, interactivity and real-time into account.

title: Processes
text:
Computing priority

Static priority: computed at creation-time, remains the same until Exit.
Easy to compute, does not reflect changes in process behaviour.
We can score interactivity by measuring how long waiting for I/O.
Longer wait means more interactivity.
Interactivity score can change during process lifetime.
Dynamic priority: recomputed regularly based on collected data.
More expensive to compute, but better reflects changing behaviour.

title: Processes
text:
Shortest Remaining Time
process with shortest (estimated) time remaining runs next.

A round-robin version of STF.
Difficult to estimate remaining time.
Works well for short jobs,
but long jobs may still be starved.



sft: shortest time first
as we discussed with stf, estimating time remaining may be computationally expensive or just hard to do.

title: Processes
text:
Least completed next
Process which has used the least number of CPU cycles goes next.

Gives each process an equal share of CPU time.
Interactive processes get lots of attention, since they use little CPU.
Starvation of long jobs.

title: Processes
text:
Highest response ratio next
Dynamic priority is computed based on the proportion of its lifetime it has spent running, i.e., \[\text{Priority} = \dfrac{\text{Total CPU cycles elapsed since creation}}{\text{Number of CPU cycles used}}.\]

Result: one process is scheduled repeatedly until priority drops below that of another.
An attempt to avoid starvation, since long jobs will (eventually) get a timeslice.
Small timeslices and frequent re-computations of priority, therefore lots of overhead.

Now we look at an algorithm which does not require estimating time remaining.

title: Processes
text:
Multilevel Feedback Queue


Multiple FIFO queues, \[Q_0,Q_1,\ldots,Q_n,\] where

\(Q_0\) has the highest priority
and \(Q_n\) the lowest.

title: Processes
text:
Multilevel Feedback Queue


Run processes in priority queue order.

I.e., no process in \(Q_1\) can run until \(Q_0\) is empty.
New process, \(P\), added to \(Q_0\), \(P\) is given a timeslice.

title: Processes
text:
Multilevel Feedback Queue


Suppose \(P\) is in \(Q_i\).

If \(P\) uses all of its timeslice, it is demoted to \(Q_{i+1}\),
If \(P\) voluntarily relinquishes before its timeslice is over, it remains in \(Q_i\).
If \(P\) blocks for I/O, it is promoted to \(Q_{i-1}\).

title: Processes
text:
Multilevel Feedback Queue

Newer, less compute-intensive processes get higher priority than older, more compute-intensive ones.
Good for responsiveness, since I/O intensive processes tend to rise.
Bad for compute-intensive processes, which tend to fall and get starved.
To avoid this, the timeslice is doubled each time a process is demoted.
Older, longer running processes occasionally get a large slice of CPU time.

Used by Windows NT and some Unix derivatives

title: Processes
text:
Traditional Unix Scheduling

used by older Unix systems,
modern UNIX schedulers are much more advanced.
A pre-emptive scheduler,
with a timer interrupt every \(1/60^{\mathrm{th}}\) of a second (about 16ms).
priority-based system.
Priority of each process based on

Base priority (more for system processes, less for user processes),
CPU usage (lower usage gives more priority),
Modifier to increase / decrease priority, called nice value.

title: Processes
text:
Traditional Unix Scheduling

Priority is a whole number: lower number means more priority.
Processes with the same priority are scheduled in a round-robin fashion.
Similar to MFQ, where each priority value is a queue level.
Processes start with a base priority, smaller number for system process, larger for user processes.
Priority can be modified by adding a nice value, a number from \(-20\) to \(+19\),
only root can set nice \(< 0\). Nice \(=-20\) can lock up the system.
Every \(1/2\) second (500ms), CPU used is halved so that it decays over time:
priority value represents only recent CPU usage.

title: Processes
text:
Drawbacks

All priorities are recomputed at once, every second.

This took a significant length of time, especially on older computers.
Priorities are not updated frequently enough to respond to changes in behaviour.
Does not scale well to systems with a large number of processes.

Modern systems have 1000s of processes,
so Traditional Unix Scheduling is no longer practical.


MFQ: multilevel feedback queue note: tied priorities and MFQ, similar but with lots more queues.

title: Processes
text:
Multi-user systems

What to do if there are multiple users?
2 users: User1 has 100 processes, User2 has only 2.
Should we give each user or each process the same amount of CPU time?
Fair Share Scheduling gives each user, group, or other entity the same mount of CPU time.

text:

Scheduling is a difficult talk;
we need to balance many priorities.
Schedulers need to gather and analyse many statistics about the process.
