title: Operating Systems
text:
What is an Operating System

Just another program.
Provides a programming interface for the computer hardware.
Responsible for managing (protecting) resources.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Managing resources

Typically hardware, e.g.,
CPU, memory, files on disk, peripherals.
Resources are limited.

embedded devices and smart devices still have small amounts of memory,
even large supercomputers are not powerful enough for scientists,
modern PCs have huge amounts of memory and processing power compared to early computers.
Many users still want more, e.g., for smooth game performance.

Resources need protecting.

title: Operating Systems
section: What protection should the OS provide?
text:
What protection should the OS provide?

Security and integrity
Prevent one user or program from corrupting another.
Authorisation
Ensures only those “allowed” have access to certain resources.
Authentication
Checking whether a user or program has the authorisation it claims to have.
Save me from myself
Protecting the user / programmer from their own stupid mistakes.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Optimise performance

In addition, operating systems ensure resources meet certain criteria.
E.g.,:

responsiveness: by prioritising certain events,
real-time: such as machinery in a factory, actuators on an aircraft,
security: by preventing accidental or malicious tampering.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Programming interface

Easier access to hardware and peripherals:
hardware programming can be fiddly and complicated.
Less repeated code:
Common tasks, e.g., file handling, are implemented.
Less chance of errors

Since the OS is written by experts.
Code is used by many people, so there is more chance of errors being found and fixed.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Written by experts

Experts understand the hardware:

understand exactly how the hardware works,
know how to get the best performance,
know the intricacies and pitfalls of hardware programming,
consider all the details, e.g., handling interrupts,




Device drivers were probably written by the hardware manufacturers themselves.
We can safely assume that expert OS developers are better programmers, and better computer scientists than us.
They likely already made most of the mistakes, and learnt from them, that less experienced programmers are likely to make.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Layered model













Splits a computer system into distinct chunks,
which interact with each other through and interface.
Modelling allows us to look at the system in an appropriate level of detail.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Layered model



Hardware: warm scone,
Cream: user-land applications, including the GUI.
Jam: operating system, providing an insulating layer between the scone and cream.
Protects the hardware from user-land applications.











A computer, applications and its operating system is like a correctly constructed scone.



We represent a computer, applications and operating system as a 3-layered model
Analogy: a correctly constructed scone. Note that jam is a good insulator and prevents the warm scone from causing the cream to melt.
Thus the OS is like the jam.

title: Operating Systems
section: Note: GUI is a user-land application
text:
Note: GUI is a user-land application

Any program the user interacts with is not part of the operating system
this is “user-land”.
The GUI (desktop environment, window manager, etc) is not part of the operating system.
As computer scientists, we should not confuse

the OS and its GUI,
the OS and the hardware it is running on.




Many people confuse the OS and the GUI, and OS and the hardware it runs on.
OS manufacturers contribute to this confusion by marketing the GUI / hardware as part of the OS.
E.g., think of Windows advertisements which emphasise the GUI, or Mac advertisements which emphasise the Apple hardware.
However, if you’ve ever used Linux, you may have come across different “flavours” of the same distribution, which include different desktop environments (GUIs).
You may also be familiar with the same OS running on different hardware. E.g., running Windows on Mac hardware, running Linux on Mac or PC hardware.
Thus, as computer scientists, we need to be clear about what the OS is:
the layer between the hardware and user-land, responsible for managing and protecting resources, as well as providing an interface to the programmer.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Separation of concerns

Layering allows us to decouple software:

device drivers (e.g., interacting with peripherals),
OS code (e.g., process scheduling, memory management),
and user interface

should be as loosely coupled as possible.



loose coupling: means the code of different components is intertwined as little as possible.
in a loosely coupled system, you should be able to swap out one component for another without needing to make many changes to the rest of the system.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Tight coupling causes problems



Huge source of bugs,
since an error in the GUI could cause the entire system to crash.
Security risk
as a malicious user could gain access to OS internals through a poorly programmed application.











The famous “blue screen of death”.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Loose coupling enables code re-use



Loose coupling allows us to swap out one component,
while making minimal changes to the rest of the system.
This allows us to re-use much of the OS code, while only changing hardware-specific drivers,
allowing the same OS to run on many devices.

The Android OS shares lots of code with the Linux kernel.

title: Operating Systems
section: A good operating system should be…
text:
A good operating system should be…

Lightweight and efficient
so that as many resources as possible can be dedicated to user-land applications.
Flexible and easy to use,
i.e., it should be a help, not a hindrance, to the programmer.

title: Operating Systems
section: Early computers did not have operating systems
text:
Early computers did not have operating systems


Programs loaded into EDSAC from paper tape,
“starting orders” helped the operator load and initialise the program.
Programmer had to know which machine they were writing code for
since each early computer was slightly different.
Had to write low-level code, interacting directly with the hardware,
e.g., each program re-implemented printing to the TTY.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Manual scheduling


Each program (job) was hung on a line,
forming a job queue.
A human operator manually loaded each program into the computer,
If the program ran successfully, its output would be returned to the programmer,
In case of an error, the operator would write the memory address at which the program failed and return this to the programmer.
Turn-around could be days, if there was an error the programmer would have to restart the process.












In the 60s, there was no such thing as hacking away at a program and re-running it until it worked. Programmers learnt to “run” the programs in their heads, read machine code from paper tape, understand oscilloscope traces or audio cues to determine if their program was running correctly. At this time there were no high-level languages, and no debuggers.

title: Operating Systems
section: Code re-use: libraries and device drivers
text:
Code re-use: libraries and device drivers

Early programmers had to re-implement everything.

writing output,
working with files,
performing maths operations such as square root.

Libraries were soon developed, so that programmers could share commonly repeated code.
To avoid low-level programming, working directly with hardware, device drivers were developed.
Linkers and loaders were then developed to give access to this shared code.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Spooling

Early computers were expensive to run.
So it was important to keep the CPU as busy as possible.
Manually loading programs became a bottleneck.
A batch of programs was loaded onto a “fast” medium (magnetic tape) and run sequentially.
This process was called spooling.
Printing output via a teleprinter was also a bottleneck,
so this was also spooled.

title: Operating Systems
text:
The Monitor

A small program which

loaded a program,
ran it on the hardware,
and wrote its output.

Directed by a special-purpose programming language called job control language.
See e.g., IBM JCL, or SLURM.

title: Operating Systems
text:
The Monitor

Also responsible for automatic accounting, prioritising e.g., users who paid more and killing processes if they exceeded allocated CPU or memory.
Still widely used in modern mainframes or time-shared supercomputers.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Multitasking

Some operations were slow and needed no CPU,
e.g., writing output.
To best utilise the CPU, multiple programs were loaded at once,
When the CPU was idle, another program could make use of it.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Multitasking

The Monitor was responsible for scheduling the programs,
i.e., deciding which should be run and when.
Note that exactly one program ran at a time.
Each program had to surrender control back to the monitor,
there was no way for the Monitor to automatically stop a rogue program.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Co-operative approach

Several programs and their data were loaded into memory.
All programs, including the Monitor, had the same rights.
One program was able to

monopolise resources by not surrendering control,
overwrite another program or its data,
overwrite the Monitor.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Early scheduling

Monitor allowed one program to run until it surrendered control.
Problem: a malicious or erroneous program could monopolise all resources.
More complicated scheduling algorithms were suggested,
but these consumed valuable resources, so simplicity was preferred.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Early scheduling

Another approach: pre-emptive scheduling.
The Monitor regularly interrupted running processes and decided what to do. I.e.,

continue running the same process,
run a different process,
kill the process if it had consumed too many resources.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Pre-emptive scheduling

More frequently:

each program gets a small slice of CPU,
appears more responsive,
lots of time spent handling interrupts, less time running user programs,
each interrupt “wakes up” the CPU, which consumes excessive power (in low-power systems where the CPU is often idle).

title: Operating Systems
text:
Pre-emptive scheduling

Less frequently:

programs appear slow, do not respond to user interactions,
compute intensive programs run bets, having more CPU time and less context switching,
less time spent running the monitor.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Thrashing

When a computer spends all its time running the Monitor and deciding what to do.
This was a common problem in early operating systems.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Potential solution

Use unequal time slices:

larger and less frequent slices given to compute-intensive programs.
smaller and more frequent slices given to interactive programs.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Resource protection

Early programs had the same rights:
everyone had equal access to all hardware.
Protection was needed,
this required hardware support.
CPU instructions were divided into two or more levels:

Unprivileged: “safe” instructions which all programs could run,
Privileged: e.g., access to peripherals, scheduling a process.

Only the Monitor could run in privileged mode.

title: Operating Systems
text:
User-land programs in privileged mode

If a user-land application tries to run a privileged operation,

CPU jumps to the Monitor,
monitor decides what to do,
perhaps allow the instruction, or kill the process if it is not allowed.

A user-land program may “politely ask” to perform a privileged operation,
by raising a system call (syscall).

title: Operating Systems
text:
Memory protection

All programs had equal access to memory.
one program could overwrite another program or its data,
or overwrite prat of the Monitor.
Protection was needed,
and this also required hardware support.
The Memory Management Unit (MMU) was responsible for this.

title: Operating Systems
text:
The Memory Management Unit

Memory divided into “pages”, typically 4096 bytes, but often larger, e.g., 4MB.
For each program, MMU stores a table of pages,
for each address, the MMU has a flag indicating whether the program can

read,
write,
or execute (run as code)

that page.

title: Operating Systems
text:
The Memory Management Unit

It is useful to separate reading, writing and executing.

Prevents one program overwriting another program or its data,
Prevents user data being treated as code (security risk),

title: Operating Systems
text:
Fast and transparent

Each access to memory must be checked by the MMU,
If a program attempts to access memory out of bounds, an interrupt is sent to the OS,
which typically kills the process (through raising a segmentation fault SIGSEGV).
this is yet another overhead. MMU must be very fast and operate transparently.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Late 60s to mid 90s

Pre-emptive scheduling and resource protection began to appear in mainframes in the late 1960s.
DOS (Disk OS), an early “home” OS was a single program OS with no pre-emption or memory protection due to lack of hardware support.
Windows 3.1 also had no pre-emption or memory protection.
Hardware support was quickly added,
by the mid 80s, Unix-derived OSs added pre-emption and memory protection.

title: Operating Systems
section: Summary: what have early computers taught us?
text:
Summary: what have early computers taught us?

Resources need managing,
since they are limited, we want to get best performance otu of hardware and best user experience.
Resources also need protection
from out or malicious programs, e.g., limiting access to memory, but also files and network.
Programmers need a convenient interface,
to best interact with hardware, avoid repeating code, and produce fewer errors.

title: Memory
text:
Objectives

title: Memory
text:
Recap: operating systems
Purpose:

to manage resources
and provide a convenient interface to the programmer.

title: Memory
text:
Recap: operating systems

So far, we have looked at processes:
code, data and metadata held by the operating system.
Typically operating systems run several (dozen, hundred) processes
OS manages processes:

Scheduling: deciding which process should run when,
Protection: ensuring that one user’s processes cannot interfere with another user’s processes,
IPC: facilitating safe communication (allowing synchronisation and data sharing between processes).

title: Memory
text:
Recap: hardware components
As well as managing processes, the OS must look after other hardware.

Von Neumann architecture is used in many modern computers.
Next, we will look at memory management.

title: Memory
text:
Purpose

Protection and management:

share out a limited resource,
ensure processes cannot interfere with each other’s memory,

programming interface:

allow processes to safely request and access memory,
do as much low-level work for the programmer as possible.

title: Memory
text:
Limited resource?

We have already discussed that everything is limited,
even in modern computers where memory is plentiful.
Wirth’s law: software is decelerating faster than hardware is accelerating.
Gates’ law: programs double in size every 18 months.

PC software such as games performs best with as many resources as possible,
Some problems in scientific computation are still to big for even the largest mainframes.

Generative AI.



Wirth’s law. as computers get faster, software can afford to run slower (be less efficient) and still run at the same speed as before. Wirth’s law states that it’s actually worse: software is slowing down more than hardware is speeding up.

title: Memory
text:
Processes and memory

Each process requires some memory

to store its code (instructions),
data, and OS metadata.

A process may request memory either at startup or while it is running.
Likewise, it may reallocate memory at any point while it is running, or when it exits.

title: Memory
text:
Memory layout



The CPU expects instructions to appear in order,
i.e., so the next one can be found by incrementing the program counter,
Program expects data to appear in one contiguous block.
Early computers allocated contiguous blocks of memory for each process.





OS (kernel)

title: Memory
text:
Evolution: static memory

The OS splits memory up into contiguous blocks called partitions.
Early machines were static,
i.e., they had a fixed number of partitions.
Each process could be a fixed size,
which the programmer would estimate at startup.
If memory was needed while the process was running, the programmer would usually over-estimate its needs.

title: Memory
text:
Evolution: static memory

Partitions may be all the same size or different sizes.

Same size could be inefficient as a big and a small process got the same allocation,
Dynamic was better, but it could be hard to find a partition to fit the upcoming process.

title: Memory
text:
Dynamic allocation

Quickly added to OS’s, then, later to high-level programming languages.
Memory is allocated as needed.
Many programming languages use implicit dynamic allocation, where memory is allocated automatically.
E.g., Java, Python, C++ strings (which are not primitive types).
Other languages use explicit dynamic allocation, where the programmer must ask the OS for a certain number of bytes,
E.g., C/C++ malloc() and free().
Both approaches have pros and cons…

title: Memory
text:
Dynamic allocation



OS implicitly allocates memory when a new process is created.
Again, contiguous blocks are needed and the size must be known at startup.
Programmers used clever tricks to squeeze more into a smaller chunk of memory.
When a process exits, it leaves a gap in memory.

A tricky problem became how best to fill the gaps.
This is known as fragmentation, and is a common problem.






OS (kernel)


P1


P2


P3


Free memory






programming trick: overlays
if all code, or all data did not fit into memory, a programmer would manually copy parts of it to / from main memory.
i.e., if some code needs to be copied, the programmer must be aware, keep track of this, and explicitly load it from disk.
extremely fiddly and easy to get wrong – required excellent programmers to do it right.
fragmentation: you’ve likely heard of this in relation to data on a hard disk drive, where the same thing happens – as files are deleted, new ones get spread out across lots of small chunks of memory.

title: Memory
text:

title: Memory
text:
Gaps in memory



When processes end, they leave gaps in memory.
A tricky problem became how to fill the gaps…

First fit: first large enough gap found.
Best fit: smallest gap large enough to accommodate it,
Worst fit: largest gap available.

Surprisingly, worst fit is the best option, since it leaves gaps large enough to be used by other processes.
Whereas the gaps left by best fit are too small for anything useful.

title: Memory
text:
Garbage collection

All data can periodically be compacted into a contiguous block.
Garbage collection periodically

Deletes data which is no longer needed,
re-organises data to get best use of space.

The operation is performed for all of memory and runs relatively often.

Takes a significant amount of time, since it’s expensive to move blocks of data around.
More overheads, less time for user processes.
Garbage collection pause is unsuitable for real-time software.

Better solutions exist (with hardware support).

title: Memory
text:
Gaps in memory

What should the OS do if there is not a big enough gap?

Refuse to admit the process,
If the new process is sufficiently important, kill other processes.
Pre-empt memory – take it away from other processes.

title: Memory
text:
Swapping

Move some data from memory to disk to free up space.
Allow other processes to use the freed memory,
copy data back from disk to memory the next time the process is scheduled.
Note that other processes may need to be swapped to allow the original one back in.
Typically, a process which is already blocked is swapped.

title: Memory
text:
Another cooking analogy



Suppose you’re cooking, but your really finicky housemate comes in.
They demand to cook immediately, but claim that there is not enough space in the kitchen.
You reluctantly pack all of your ingredients back into the fridge and your cupboard.
Your housemate uses the now free work surface to cook an elaborate meal which they do not share.

title: Memory
text:
Convenient programming interface

Similar idea to overlays,
This time, copying code and data to and from memory is handled by the OS.
Programmers should still be aware,
since they should try to avoid swapping.

title: Memory
text:
Swapping

The OS must decide which process(es) to swap.
E.g., several small ones, or one large one.
Part of the problem of medium-term scheduling:
deciding what to load into memory for the short-term scheduler to consider.

title: Memory
text:
Swapping

I/O vs compute intensive?

I/O processes require occasional small timeslices but a fast response,
therefore waiting for a swap may be unacceptable.
Compute processes require longer timeslices and want to be run now,
the swap time is less critical, but these processes want to be run immediately.

Another trade-off for the OS to consider.

title: Memory
text:
Pages

We tend to swap collections of pages rather than collections of bytes.
A page is a contiguous block of memory,
Hardware can copy pages to and from memory very quickly and efficiently.
Recall that processes require a contiguous block of memory.
Sometimes there is sufficient memory, but it is fragmented.
Random Access Memory means any byte can be accessed in a constant time,
unlike mechanical hard disk drives, where data far apart takes longer to read.

title: Memory
text:
Pages

We can solve the problem of fragmentation by making it look like the process has a contiguous block even if it does not:
virtual memory.
The OS creates a mapping from physical page addresses to virtual page addresses,
Every process gets a virtual contiguous block, regardless of the physical location of pages.

title: Memory
text:
Page tables



A page table maps virtual pages currently in use by each process to their physical memory addresses.
Provides isolation and memory protection:
since each process gets its own virtual page space, it can only access memory the OS allows it to.














the page table contains page mappings, i.e., virtual address x ==> physical address y, rather than pages themselves.
tables consume memory, so should be kept as small as possible. this is why only memory in current use is tracked.
providing each process with its own set of virtual pages gives the illusion that each process has exclusive access to all of memory. the OS can then enforce memory protection (if a process tries to access memory out of bounds) and isolation (since it can ensure virtual addresses for each process point to different areas of memory).

title: Memory
text:
Overheads?

Suppose a process wants to read a value from memory, increment it and then write the result to a different location.
The OS must:

Look up the physical address of data in the page table,
Fetch the value,
Perform the increment,
Look up the physical address of the new location in tho page table,
Write the value to memory.
Since instructions are stored in memory, too, the page table must be checked for every instruction fetch as well!

We’ve now doubled the number of slow memory accesses!

title: Memory
text:
Hardware support: the TLB



Very fast area of memory which stores a section of the page table.
Fast memory is expensive so it can only hold a small number of mappings.
Sits between the CPU and main memory and automatically translates virtual to physical addresses.

title: Memory
text:
Hit or Miss

Suppose the CPU does a fetch from memory.
The TLB attempts to translate virtual to physical address.

Hit: mapping found, fetch from physical address,
Miss: need to search the page table (another read from memory) for the mapping.
New mapping is loaded into the TLB and the fetch continues.

This can be done entirely in hardware, which is fast and transparent to the OS.
If there is no hardware support, a TLB miss interrupt is raised and the OS must implement and manage this process.

title: Memory
text:
TLB misses

A search through the page table to find a mapping which is missing from the TLB is called a page walk.
If there is a TLB miss and no mapping in the page table, the OS may

allocate a new page, storing its mapping in the page table,
refuse to allocate the new page: raises a segmentation violation (SIGSEGV)




when no mapping is found, this is called a “page fault”.
a TLB miss is often called a “minor” page fault. With hardware support, this can be handled independently from the OS.
a TLB miss plus no mapping in the page table cannot be handled in hardware, and needs intervention by the OS. This is called a “major” page fault, and an interrupt is always sent to the OS.
what really happens in the OS?

process instruction says read from memory address x.
TLB checks for a mapping, but none is found. minor page fault is raised.
with hardware support, automatic page walk is performed. if the mapping is found in the page table, then it is placed in the TLB and the fetch continues.
if no mapping is found in the page table, a major page fault interrupt is raised.
current process is de-scheduled, and OS code begins to run.
If the OS decides not to allocate a new page, it sens a SIGSEGV (segmentation violation signal) to the process. Next time the process is scheduled, this signal will be handled and the process will be terminated.
if the OS decides it will allocate a new page, the mapping is placed in the page table. next time the process is scheduled, the pgae walk is repeated, but this time the mapping will be fonud and the fetch will go ahead.

title: Memory
text:
Exercise: hardware support

x86 processors have hardware support,
Spark and MIPS processors do not.
Find out whether the processor in…

the computer you’re currently using, your smartphone, and
any other smart devices you have (e.g., watch, TV, speaker)

has hardware support for handling minor page faults.

title: Memory
text:
TLB misses

A search through the page table to find a mapping which is missing from the TLB is called a page walk.
If there is a TLB miss and no mapping in the page table,
a page fault interrupt is raised.
The OS may decide to allocate a new page or send a segmentation violation signal to the process.
Even with hardware support, a page walk is expensive.
A major page fault, causing an interrupt, is even more so.
We want to have as few TLB misses as possible!

title: Memory
text:
Paging: swapping pages

Page tables give us a convenient way of providing
contiguous blocks of memory as well as memory protection and process isolation.
Pages can also be swapped to disk.
All done automatically by the OS,
but the OS has to decide which pages to throw out.

title: Memory
text:
Paging strategies

Which pages should the OS throw out?

Random: pick any.

title: Memory
text:
Paging strategies

Random:
Simple, surprisingly effective.
FIFO: first page loaded is first thrown out.

title: Memory
text:
Paging strategies

(FIFO:
Poor, since pages which have been around for a long time tend to be needed.
Least recently used: throw out the page accessed the longest time ago.

title: Memory
text:
Paging strategies

Least Recently used
Works well, but needs hardware support.
Least frequently used: keep a count of accesses, the page with fewest accesses is thrown out.

title: Memory
text:
Paging strategies

Least frequently used
Poor because newly loaded pages tend to get thrown out immediately.



the most efficient option is least recently used.
TLB and page table now needs an extra storage space to track last access time.
“pages which have been around the longest tend to be most used” - most programs tend to declare some variables and use them throughout. A program which creates lots of variables and accesses memory all over the place can cause lots of TLB misses and run more slowly than a conventionally written program.

title: Memory
text:
Lazy allocation and contiguous blocks

Each time a process requests a new page,
the OS simply takes the next available in memory.
Virtual mapping takes care of creating a contiguous block.
Pages are only allocated when needed – lazy allocation,
only memory used is allocated, solves the problem of over-allocation.
Unlike with overlays, which were completely manual,
paging has abstracted all the complexity away from the programmer.
Programmers should still be aware of how things work,
and write programs accordingly (e.g., to avoid swapping).

title: Memory
text:
Context-switching

Each process has its own page table.
When a context-switch happens, the TLB should be cleared.
Most of the cost in context-switching comes from repopulating the TLB.
More sophisticated TLB also store the process ID,
lookup is based on virtual address and process ID, no longer needs clearing.

title: Memory
text:
Shared memory

Shared memory can easily be set up:
simply map virtual addresses for multiple processes to the same physical locations.
Code can be shared, too – shared libraries.
E.g., the printf function is likely used by lots of processes.

Each process maps to the same printf instructions.
Reduces overall memory use,
also reduces TLB misses as it is often looked up.

title: Memory
text:
Shared memory

Copy-on-write: if several processes share data, but few of them modify it.

Map to the shared data,
If modified, write back to a new location in memory, reserved for that process.
Efficient, but adds complexity.




a clever copy-on-write trick: zeros
many programs request a large chunk of fresh memory, initialised with zeros (can be done using the calloc function).
Thus, the OS keeps a large chuck of memory full of zeros ready for this purpose.
rather than setting aside all the memory at once, the process is simply given a reference to this huge pool of zeros.
due to copy-on-write, if the program modifies any of the memory, they are allocated their own copy, but only of the parts it has changed.
this can be really efficient, e.g., when working with sparse matrices (2d arrays in which most of the values are zero).

title: Memory
text:
Spooling

Spooling: early computers would write data to memory, and the OS would schedule printing later.
Virtual memory can be mapped to anything:
files, I/O devices, e.g., sound cards.
Process accesses the devices by “writing to memory”,
OS can handle this in the most efficient way.



note: this is more convenience for the programmer as they don’t have to worry about hardware or technicalities of writing to different devices or files, they only need to know how to access memory.

title: Memory
text:
Memory discrepancy

The CPU runs at 1000s of MHz (GHz),
Memory may run at a few 100s of MHz,
Accessing memory is orders of magnitude slower than the CPU can run.
The time taken to access memory is also very long (latency).
We could add many parallel channels connecting the CPU and memory,
this allows more throughput, but doesn’t fix the latency.

title: Memory
text:
Registers and cache

Registers are small chunks of memory on the CPU itself,
typically used to store intermediate values.
A cache is a small, fast chunk of memory which sits between the CPU and main memory,
used to store frequently used values.
Access to memory goes through the cache:

if the data is in the cache, it is returned very quickly,
otherwise, it is fetched from memory,
done automatically, transparent from the OS.

title: Memory
text:
Memory hierarchy

Since faster memory is more expensive, we often have multiple levels of cache,
each level, further from the CPU, is larger and slower.

title: Memory
text:
Recap

Computer architecture broken down into 5 components: ALU, Control Unit, Memory, Input and Output.
VNA has shared memory for instructions and data
Harvard has separate memory for instructions and data.

title: Memory
text:
Multi-processor architecture

So far we have considered only single-processor architectures,
but almost all modern computers include multiple processors (or multiple cores).
Each processor may have its own cache, but we need to keep cached values consistent across CPUs.
A shared cache solves this problem, but causes a bottleneck.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Optimising the fetch-decode-execute-store cycle

Suppose the CPU can perform one stage per CPU cycle.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Von Neumann architecture is sequential

Suppose the computer can perform one stage per CPU cycle.
The ALU is only working during the Execute stage.
It would be ideal to have the ALU doing work all the time.
We’ll look at three ways of getting the best use out of the hardware.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Pipelines
Overlap stages of the fetch-decode-execute-store cycle.

ALU receives a constant stream of work.

Instruction pipelining is a bit like a production line. Each piece of hardware has its designated job – Control unit for decoding, ALU for executing. Once an instruction is decoded, it is passed to the ALU for execution, while the ALU executes the instruction, the Control unit is decoding the next. This means the ALU is not sitting idle while the control unit decodes instructions for it.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Speedup
In a sequential fetch, decode, execute, store cycle, it takes 4 cycles for each instruction to complete.

40 cycles for 10 instructions.
In a pipelined architecture:

It takes 4 cycles for the first instruction to exit the pipeline.
5 cycles for the second
6 for the third,
… and so on …
14 for the 10-th instruction to exit the pipeline.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Speedup
\[
S_n = \dfrac{\text{Time to complete } n \text{ tasks sequentially}}{\text{Time to complete} n \text{ tasks in a pipeline}}
\]

The speedup for 10 instructions in a 4 stage pipeline is \[
S_10 = \dfrac{40}{14} \approx 2.86
\]
The more instructions, the better! \[
S_{100} = \dfrac{400}{104} \approx 3.51, S_{1000} = \dfrac{1000}{1014} = 3.94
\]

For a pipeline with \(k\) stages, speedup approaches \(k\) as the number of instructions grows very large.

Mathematical explanation:

Suppose we have \(n\) instructions to complete.
For a pipeline with \(k\) stages:

The first operation leaves the pipeline after \(k\) cycles.
The \(n\)-th instruction leaves the pipeline after \(k + n\) cycles.

\(T_{\mathrm{pipeline}} = k + n\) CPU cycles.
Without pipelining, each stage is completed sequentially for each instruction.
\(T_{\mathrm{seq}} = k \cdot n\) CPU cycles.
We can calculate speedup, a measure of how much quicker the pipelines system is: \[S = \dfrac{T_{\mathrm{seq}}}{T_{\mathrm{pipeline}}} = \dfrac{k \cdot n}{k + n}.\]
Pipelines work best for a large number of tasks: \(n \gg k\).
Then \(S = k\).

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Throughput and latency

Throughput: Number of instructions completed per unit time.

\(\text{Throughput} = \dfrac{\text{number of instructions}}{\text{execution time}}\)
Higher throughput indicates better performance.

Latency: time taken for a single instruction to complete (travel through the pipeline)

\(\text{Latency} = \dfrac{\text{execution time}}{\text{number of instructions}}\)
Lower latency indicates better performance.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Pipelines


Advantages

Higher throughput: more instructions per second
Better hardware utilisation: reduces idle time.
Well-suited to repetitive tasks.


Disadvantages

Higher latency: time taken to complete one instruction
More complex: increases design complexity, manufacture cost and, therefore, time.
Works most efficiently when kept full.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Pipeline hazards

Situations which cause the pipeline to stall, or have to restart.
Control dependency: which instructions should be pipelines after a jump?
Data hazards: when data dependence affecting instructions at different stages of the pipeline.

One instruction may depend on the result of a previous instruction still in the pipeline.
Read after write: one instruction attempts to read data which another instruction has not yet written.
Write after read: one instruction writes data after another instruction attempts to read it.
Write after write: one instruction attempts to write data after another, messing up register values.




control dependency: after a jump instruction, instructions may need to be loaded from a new location of memory. It is unknown, at the time the jump enters the pipeline, what its outcome will be, therefore the correct sequence of instructions cannot be pipelines.

Processors employ branch prediction to guess whether a jump is likely to happens or not. The “most likely” sequence of instructions are pipelined, meaning there is a high probability that the correct instructions are loaded into the pipeline. However, if branch prediction is incorrect, then the pipeline must be restarted, as different instructions need to be fetched, decoded, etc.

Data dependencies: one instruction may depend upon the result of another, so it must wait (stall) until its dependant has left the pipeline. Now we have a “bubble” (empty gap) in the pipeline.

There may be contention over registers wherein one instruction attempts to read or write to registers, or cache, being used by another. In this case, a calculation may have to be restarted, or at least the correct data loaded from memory (slowwww) again.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism

Some CPUs have multiple ALUs, or special-purpose hardware.
We want all of this hardware to be working all of the time.
However, we need to figure out which operations can be re-ordered or executed in parallel.

Example: Euclidean distance

Suppose we have two points, \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) in 2d space, e.g., in a 2d game.
To calculate the distance between \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1,x_2)\) and \(\mathbf{y} = (y_1,y_2)\), we use Pythagoras’ theorem.
Euclidean distance, \(D = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\).
Let \(x_1 = 4, x_2 = 9, y_1 = 20, y_2 = 11\).


Don’t worry about the actual formula. It’s only important to note we have a square root, two multiplications, and an addition.

CPU can add, mul, sub and sqrt in a single CPU cycle.

t1 = x2 - x1
t2 = t1 * t1
t3 = y1 - y2
t4 = t3 * t3

D = sqrt( t5 )

t1 and t3 can be computed

t5 must wait for t2 and t4,
The result, D depends on t5.

Four principles:

Make each program do one thing well. To do a new job, build afresh rather than complicate old programs by adding new “features”.

title: Deadlock
text:
Recap: the process lifecycle

One process may ask the OS to create a new one (fork or spawn),
OS creates a process in the new state.
When a process is initialised, the OS moves it to the ready state.
The OS may decide to schedule (dispatch) a ready process,
its state is changed to running and any saved data is restored (MMU, registers).
if a process requires I/O, it requests this from the OS via a syscall,
OS sets its state to blocked until the I/O is done, then its state i set to ready.

title: Deadlock
text:

A running process may be interrupted or pre-empted,
then its data is saved and state changed to ready.
When a process is finished, its state is set to exit,
the OS does some cleanup before the process is deleted.

Recap: scheduling
Deciding what to do next.
A good scheduler should:

not give any process too much CPU, but
not give any process too little, either (starvation).
Give compute-heavy processes longer, larger slices of CPU time, but
give interactive processes small slices of CPU time very often.
Ensure real-time (safety-critical) processes run immediately.

Optimise for different types of hardware, e.g.,
mice and printers are slow, network and disk is (comparatively) fast.
Provide predictable behaviour, and
degrade gracefully under excessive load.
Run fast, so as to maximise time spent running user-land applications
and avoid thrashing.


Note that other other resources, e.g., I/O, need scheduling, too.
Different resource schedulers may disagree about which process to run next.

title: Deadlock
text:
The OS also needs to

prevent deadlocks,
a group of processes all waiting for one of their number to do something.
Process protection:
insuring that processes cannot interfere with one another.

title: Deadlock
text:
Example



Process \(P_1\) wants copy to a file from disk \(A\) to disk \(B\).
Process \(P_2\) wants to copy a file from disk \(B\) to disk \(A\).
Only one process can access the disk at any one time.

What happens?











Example



\(P_1\) is scheduled.
\(P_1\) is given disk \(A\),
Now \(P_2\) is scheduled.
It is given access to disk \(B\).
\(P_2\) is still running.
It requests access to disk \(A\).
Request is denied since \(P_1\) has disk \(A\).
\(P_2\) blocks, waiting for disk \(A\).














Example

\(P_1\) is scheduled.
It requests access to disk \(B\).
The request is denied since \(P_2\) has disk \(B\) already.
\(P_1\) blocks waiting for disk \(B\).
Now both \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are blocked.
Only \(P_1\) can unblock \(P_2\), and only \(P_2\) can unblock \(P_1\).

We have a deadlock.


Formal definition: deadlock
A group of processes, \(D = \{P_1,\ldots,P_k\}\) is deadlocked if

every process \(P_i\) is blocked, waiting for an event \(E_i\),
but the event \(E_i\) can only be caused by a process in \(D\).


Skip the maths



Definition: Deadlock
A group of processes is deadlockd if:

Every process is waiting for an event to happen
But only another process in the group can trigger the event.



Coffman conditions

Mutual exclusion:
exclusive access to a resource is required.j
Hold and wait:
a process holds onto a resource while waiting for another.
No pre-emption:
once a process has a resource, it cannot be taken away.

A deadlock is only possible if all three conditions are met.


Exercise
How are the three conditions met in the disk writing example we considered earlier?

Process \(P_1\) wants to copy a file from disk \(A\) to disk \(B\).
Process \(P_2\) wants to copy a file from disk \(B\) to disk \(A\).
Only one process can access the disk at any one time.



“Only one process can access the disk”: mutual exclusion. Usually it’s hard to break this one.
In the example, both processes grab the disks and hang onto them while they wait for the other to let it go.
No pre-emption: there is no mechanism to force either process to drop the disk.




Deadlock prevention

If we break at least one Coffman condition, deadlock is impossible.
Seems possible, but maybe harder than it looks…



Prevent hold and wait

Hold and wait
process holds onto a resource while waiting for another.
Solution:
each time a process blocks on a resource, they must drop all other resources.
Drawback
process has to request all resources again.
It may never be possible to grab all resources at once.



Prevent hold and wait

Why not block until all resources become available?

Inefficient, since the process could have been doing useful work in the meantime.
Process may not need all resources at the same time – some other process could have been using them.
A process may not know what resources it needs at startup, so this could be impossible.

an even stricter approach: start the process only when resources are available.
Process releases resources when it exits.



not knowing resource needs at startup. a word processor may always need disk access, but might only need printer access sometimes, and for a short period of the time it spends open.
an even stricter solution: don’t even allow the process to start until all resources are available. process then grabs resources and releases them when completed.

what are the potential drawbacks of this solution?
similar to previous, also
2hr computation plus 20s write to disk. process has exclusive access to the disk for its entire 2:00:20 running time (during which, of course, no other process can access the disk).





Prevent mutual exclusion



Mutual exclusion:
a process requires exclusive access to a resource.
Solution:
allow multiple devices to access the same resource at the same time.
Drawback often impossible.
E.g., printer, mechanical hard disk drive with one read/write head.














prevent mutual exclusion

Alternative solution: virtual resources.

Process appears to have exclusive access to a resource, while OS is storing the operations to be performed later.
Early example: spooling – process writes to magnetic tape, later OS prints out paper tape. Process does not have to wait for [access to] the printer.




Prevent No pre-emption

No Pre-emption
once a process has a resource, it cannot be taken away.
Solution:
take resources away as needed.
Drawback
process expects the resource to be in the same state as when it was taken away.
We need to take care to save and restore the state or resources,
so that the process can resume working on them as before.



sometimes easy, as we will see with memory
sometimes difficult or impossible, e.g., with a printer.




Dining philosophers and the circular wait



12 philosophers sit around a table,
They want to share a bowl of noodles, eaten with chopsticks.
Each philosopher has one chopstick to the left and one chopstick to the right of their plate:
a philosopher needs two chopsticks to eat.

There are not enough chopsticks to go around.













Dining philosophers and the circular wait
The Coffman conditions all hold!

Mutual exclusion: one chopstick can be used by at most one philosopher at a time.
Hold and wait: a greedy philosopher will not put down a chopstick once they have picked it up.
No pre-emption: no waiter has ever been brave enough to take a chopstick from a hungry philosopher!

The disk writing deadlock was an example of circular wait.


Preventing Circular Wait

Circular wait
each process in a circle is waiting for a resource that the next process has.
Solution

Put an order on resources, e.g., \(\underbrace{M_{1}<\cdots<M_{k}}_{\text{memory}}<\underbrace{D_{1}<\ldots<D_{\ell}}_{\text{disks}}<\underbrace{P_{1}<\cdots<P_{m}}_{\text{printers}}\).
A process can only access resources greater than the ones it already has.




How does this prevent circular wait?

Suppose \(P_1\) has \(D_1\) and wants \(D_2\).
It requests and gets access to $D_1 < \(D_2\).
It is impossible, if \(P_2\) has \(D_2\) for it to get \(D_1\), since \(D_1 < D_2\).

Circular dependencies are no longer possible.

Same problems as with preventing hold-and-wait.

Inefficient use of hardware,
resources unknown so cannot request in ascending order,
sometimes degrades to “request all resources at once”.




Avoidance

Don’t let a situation arise where deadlock is possible.
I.e., a request is refused if granting it could cause deadlock now or later.
This is hard to do, since it’s impossible to predict the future.



Dijkstra’s Banker Algorithm

Deadlock prevention algorithm based on the idea of a banker lending money.
Each request must be

feasible: can be granted,
e.g., it is impossible to allocate 100GB of memory if the computer has only 16GB.
Safe: there is no chance of deadlock if the request is granted.

A very cautious approach:
Maybe we get lucky 9/10 times and no deadlock happens, but the Banker will never grant the request.



Limitations
The algorithm requires

A fixed number of resources, which is often, but not always, true,
A fixed number of processes, which is rare in a modern PC (no new processes, no processes can exit),
Each process needs to know its maximum needs in advance.
Safety decision is computationally intensive, and gets harder as more resources are added.
Potentially inefficient use of resources due to the cautious approach.



Detection and breaking

It seems almost impossible to break the Coffman Conditions,
Prevention, e.g., using the banker’s algorithm, is limited and computationally difficult,
Maybe it’s easier and cheaper to spot deadlocks an fix them when they happen.



Deadlock detection
Earliest method:

Detection by operator,
i.e., the operator notices the computer is hanging.
EDSAC had an audio output, experienced operators could “hear” an infinite loop.



Resource Request and Allocation Graphs RRAGs
A visual representation of requests and allocations or resources,
allows us to easily spot deadlocks.

Processes are represented by squares,












RRAGs

Resources are represented by squares (number represents how many of this resource there are),












RRAGs

Requests by arrows from process to resource,












RRAGs

Allocations by arrows from resources to processes,

an even stricter solution: don’t even allow the process to start until all resources are available. process then grabs resources and releases them when completed.

what are the potential drawbacks of this solution?
similar to previous, also
2hr computation plus 20s write to disk. process has exclusive access to the disk for its entire 2:00:20 running time (during which, of course, no other process can access the disk).

title: Deadlock
text:
Prevent mutual exclusion



Mutual exclusion:
a process requires exclusive access to a resource.
Solution:
allow multiple devices to access the same resource at the same time.
Drawback often impossible.
E.g., printer, mechanical hard disk drive with one read/write head.

title: Deadlock
text:
prevent mutual exclusion

Alternative solution: virtual resources.

Process appears to have exclusive access to a resource, while OS is storing the operations to be performed later.
Early example: spooling – process writes to magnetic tape, later OS prints out paper tape. Process does not have to wait for [access to] the printer.

title: Deadlock
text:
Prevent No pre-emption

No Pre-emption
once a process has a resource, it cannot be taken away.
Solution:
take resources away as needed.
Drawback
process expects the resource to be in the same state as when it was taken away.
We need to take care to save and restore the state or resources,
so that the process can resume working on them as before.



sometimes easy, as we will see with memory
sometimes difficult or impossible, e.g., with a printer.

title: Deadlock
section: Dining philosophers and the circular wait
text:
Dining philosophers and the circular wait



12 philosophers sit around a table,
They want to share a bowl of noodles, eaten with chopsticks.
Each philosopher has one chopstick to the left and one chopstick to the right of their plate:
a philosopher needs two chopsticks to eat.

There are not enough chopsticks to go around.

title: Deadlock
section: Dining philosophers and the circular wait
text:
Dining philosophers and the circular wait
The Coffman conditions all hold!

Mutual exclusion: one chopstick can be used by at most one philosopher at a time.
Hold and wait: a greedy philosopher will not put down a chopstick once they have picked it up.
No pre-emption: no waiter has ever been brave enough to take a chopstick from a hungry philosopher!

The disk writing deadlock was an example of circular wait.

title: Deadlock
text:
Preventing Circular Wait

Circular wait
each process in a circle is waiting for a resource that the next process has.
Solution

Put an order on resources, e.g., \(\underbrace{M_{1}<\cdots<M_{k}}_{\text{memory}}<\underbrace{D_{1}<\ldots<D_{\ell}}_{\text{disks}}<\underbrace{P_{1}<\cdots<P_{m}}_{\text{printers}}\).
A process can only access resources greater than the ones it already has.

title: Deadlock
section: How does this prevent circular wait?
text:
How does this prevent circular wait?

Suppose \(P_1\) has \(D_1\) and wants \(D_2\).
It requests and gets access to $D_1 < \(D_2\).
It is impossible, if \(P_2\) has \(D_2\) for it to get \(D_1\), since \(D_1 < D_2\).

Circular dependencies are no longer possible.

Same problems as with preventing hold-and-wait.

Inefficient use of hardware,
resources unknown so cannot request in ascending order,
sometimes degrades to “request all resources at once”.

title: Deadlock
text:
Avoidance

Don’t let a situation arise where deadlock is possible.
I.e., a request is refused if granting it could cause deadlock now or later.
This is hard to do, since it’s impossible to predict the future.

title: Deadlock
text:
Dijkstra’s Banker Algorithm

Deadlock prevention algorithm based on the idea of a banker lending money.
Each request must be

feasible: can be granted,
e.g., it is impossible to allocate 100GB of memory if the computer has only 16GB.
Safe: there is no chance of deadlock if the request is granted.

A very cautious approach:
Maybe we get lucky 9/10 times and no deadlock happens, but the Banker will never grant the request.

title: Deadlock
text:
Limitations
The algorithm requires

A fixed number of resources, which is often, but not always, true,
A fixed number of processes, which is rare in a modern PC (no new processes, no processes can exit),
Each process needs to know its maximum needs in advance.
Safety decision is computationally intensive, and gets harder as more resources are added.
Potentially inefficient use of resources due to the cautious approach.

title: Deadlock
text:
Detection and breaking

It seems almost impossible to break the Coffman Conditions,
Prevention, e.g., using the banker’s algorithm, is limited and computationally difficult,
Maybe it’s easier and cheaper to spot deadlocks an fix them when they happen.

title: Deadlock
text:
Deadlock detection
Earliest method:

Detection by operator,
i.e., the operator notices the computer is hanging.
EDSAC had an audio output, experienced operators could “hear” an infinite loop.

Request: Process P1 requests resource R1.

\(R1\) is already allocated to \(P1\).
Therefore \(P2\) is not allocated \(R1\).

Example: circular wait


\(R1\) allocated to \(P1\); \(R2\) allocated to \(P2\).
\(P1\) then requests \(R2\) and \(P2\) requests \(R1\).
Neither request can be fulfilled.

title: Deadlock
text:
Breaking deadlock

When a deadlock is detected, we know

the processes involved, and
the resources involved.

But how can we break the deadlock?

Kill the processes,

but which of the deadlocking processes to kill?

Take the resource away
it may be possible to fix the deadlock by taking only some the resources away from some of the processes.




the art is to kill as few processes and pre-empt as few resources as we can, but this is quite difficult.

text:

title: Deadlock
text:
A better solution: virtualisation

A computer can create almost limitless “virtual” resources,
e.g., virtual memory, printers, disks.
Process uses them as though they are true resources.
Later, the OS performs the operations done on the virtual resources on the real thing.
New problem: resource scheduling. E.g., how to write data to disk most efficiently.



with a mechanical HDD, having one write head, we can write most efficiently if the head moves around as little as possible.
therefore, writes were re-ordered so that they could be performed most efficiently.

title: Deadlock
text:
Priorities and no pre-emption

Some resources cannot be pre-empted,
e.g., if their state cannot be restored or the operation is destructive.
Suppose a low priority process has a resource which a high priority process is blocking on.
High priority process must wait for the low priority process to finish with the resource.
However the low priority process is scheduled infrequently.
In effect, the high priority process has been given lower priority than the low priority process.

This situation is called priority inversion.

title: Deadlock
text:
Resource protection

One of the main goals of the operating system.
Prevents accidental or malicious damage to resources,
e.g., corruption of other programs or data.
Now we need to ensure that one process cannot interfere with another.
More precisely, one user’s process cannot interfere with those belonging to another user.

title: Deadlock
text:
Users

Each user has a user ID, a whole number.
Resources or processes can be owned by a certain user,
by flagging them with the user’s ID.
Recall process spawning. The process which requested creation becomes the parent,
new process also inherits the user ID.
A process can make a syscall, requesting a resource,
but the request can only be granted if the resource is owned by the same user as the process.

title: Deadlock
text:
Advantages

Provides isolation, since a user can only mess with their own processes.
Security, since malware can only infiltrate one user’s programs and data.

In some operating systems, e.g., early Windows, many programs were run as admin.
This gave potential malware access to everything.

title: Deadlock
text:
The Root User

Operating systems include a special user,
often called admin, superuser or root.
This user has access to all resources and can signal all processes,
i.e., can kill processes belonging to any user.
The admin user can often do things ordinary users cannot, e.g.,

turn off the system,
delete OS files,
mess around with network configuration.

Admin user is a similar idea to privileged mode,
Note that the admin user’s instructions are still unprivileged – only OS code is privileged.

title: Deadlock
section: With great power comes great responsibility
text:
With great power comes great responsibility

It is best to spend as little time as possible as the admin user,
this reduces the risk of accidental damage or security vulnerabilities destroying your system.

# sudo rm -fr /* # removes all the French files??
# alias please=sudo # ask the OS politely to do the thing.

title: Deadlock
text:
Bootstrapping

The admin user can create any process.
When an ordinary user logs in,

admin user creates a new process,
then changes the user ID to that of the new user,
all the new user’s processes can be spawned from that one, inheriting its user ID.

title: Deadlock
text:
Capabilities

Offers finer, more granular control over resources,
e.g.,

read / modify certain areas of memory or files on disk,
access to the network, ability to install software or shutdown the computer.

This can be system wide, or as granular as per-file.
To work efficiently, hardware support is required.

title: Deadlock
text:
Permissions

The idea of capabilities never took off.
Smartphones now have permissions, which use a similar idea.
User has to grant access to filesystem / location / camera on a per-app basis.
A great idea in principle, but depends on a knowledgeable user.
Many smartphone users are novices and they can easily accidentally grant access to malicious apps.
See also polkit in Linux.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Latches

Component which “remembers” a value until it is changed by a new signal.
Can be used to store \(1\) bit of data.
Widely used in digital circuits, e.g., for data storage, control and flip-flop circuits.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
SR-latch



Set-reset latches are the simplest type of latch.
Can be constructed from two NOR gates.
Two inputs, \(S\) (set) and \(R\) (reset). State is changed when a pulse (high voltage, or \(1\)) is applied to \(S\) or \(R\).
The output is \(Q\) and its inverse is \(\overline{Q}\).

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
SR-latch












Initial state: no voltage to \(S\) or \(R\).



\(Q\) shows \(1\), its inverse, \(\overline{Q}\) shows \(0\).
To reset, apply a pulse to \(R\).
\(Q\) set to \(0\) and \(\overline{Q}\) set to \(1\).
To set the latch, apply a pulse to \(S\).
\(Q\) is set \(1\) and \(\overline{Q}\) set to \(0\).
Applying a pulse to both \(Q\) and \(R\) is not valid.

Gated SR latch



We may only want the state to change if the latch is enabled.
This can be done by building a gated latch.
Recall that an AND gate is only true when both inputs are true.
So we add AND gates, creating another input, \(E\).



The state can only change if \(E\) has a high voltage applied to it.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Application: switch bounce

Latches are widely used in electrical engineering as well as electronic computers.
When a mechanical switch is pressed, it may cause several pulses to be sent.
An SR-latch ensures that only one signal is sent, since subsequent pulses to \(S\) or \(R\) will not cause a change in state.

A gated latch can be used when state should only be changed when a device is Enabled.



E.g., an air conditioning unit may switch cooling on and off depending on input from a temperature sensor, but the unit should only switch on cooling if it has been turned on by the user.

text:
D-latch



0Data or transparent latches have two inputs: Data (\(D\)) and Enable (\(E\)).
The state changes to the value of \(D\) only when \(E\) signal is high.
When the Enable signal is low, the value of \(D\) is stored until the leading edge of the next rising Enable Signal.



A D-latch can be built from a gated SR-latch.

Flip-flops

Latches are inexpensive and easy to implement using simple logic components.
However, their behaviour can be unpredictable owing to a lack of synchronisation.
Flip-flops add a clack to synchronise their operaton.
A gated latch can be converted into a flip-flop by connecting a clock to the Enable input.

If a high pulse is sent to both \(J\) and \(K\), then the state is toggled.
I.e., \(0\) becomes \(1\) and \(1\) becomes \(0\).

Numbers are encoded in binary using a certain number of binary digits (bits).
A whole (integer) number is typically represented using \(8\) bits (a byte).
E.g., for unsigned (\(\ge 0\)) integers, \(0 = 00000000\), \(37 = 00100101\).
